News.title: Huge fire breaks out as residents forced to evacuate after ‘blast blows roof off building’
News.content:
Next

A MAJOR fire has broken out at an industrial unit as nearby residents were urgently evacuated after a “large explosion”.

Ten fire engines were sent to the farm in Sittingbourne, Kent, after the blaze broke out yesterday at around 3.30pm.



According to local residents, thick black smoke could be seen for miles.

Videos show the rising flames engulfing Tonge Corner Farm, believed to house at least five businesses.



The fire started off inside a metal barn, but quickly grew after the roof allegedly blew off.

Firefighters were forced to turn to foam to put out the flames after water was not working.



Supporting the team is a height vehicle, bulk water carrier, and firefighting robot.

It is also understood the local power grid has been switched off in fears of a larger explosion.



At least 10 properties currently do not have access to any power as firefighters were concerned the flames would reach the nearby electricity pylons.

The flames have been reduced thanks to emergency services and now just four fire trucks remain.

Locals have been quick to express their concerns over the blaze, with many reporting seeing a rush of ambulances and fire engines.

One person said: “Flames are well above the houses from where I can see.”

Another said: “There’s loads of black smoke.”



A third said: “I hope nobody is seriously hurt.”

A spokesperson for Kent Fire and Rescue Service said: “Firefighters are currently at the scene of a barn fire at Tonge Corner Road in Tonge, Sittingbourne.

“At the height of the incident, ten fire engines, a height vehicle and a bulk water carrier were sent to the scene.

“Crews have made good progress extinguishing the fire, and the incident is now being scaled down to four fire engines. The firefighting robot is also being used to reach parts of the building that firefighters cannot safely access.

“The KFRS Volunteer Response Team is also in attendance, carrying out welfare checks on nearby residents who have lost power.”

News.title: Ukraine lands direct hit on Putin’s war factory producing components for deadly ballistic warheads
News.content:
Next

UKRAINE hit a Russian war factory yesterday using British-made Storm Shadow missiles.

The key complex in Oryol produced components for the deadly ballistic warheads unleashed on Kyiv this week.



The strike on the Proton-Electrotex facility caused a massive fireball and comes after the UK agreed to send more bunker-busters to Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Kyiv’s access to Elon Musk‘s Starlink and Starshield satellite internet network have been fully restored.



Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed restrictions imposed on drones using the votal SpaceX technology had been lifted.

Mr Zelensky said: “Now we have the speed we need.

“This is very important; it is significant for our frontline logistics and for protecting Ukraine from jet-powered Shahed drones.”

It comes after US First Lady Melania Trump brokered a temporary ceasefire deal to open up evacuation routes for residents trapped in an occupied Ukrainian city.



She led round-the-clock negotiations to secure a localised truce after harrowing reports of a major humanitarian crisis in Oleshky.

Up to 6,000 residents, including hundreds of kids, have been left on the brink of starvation after months without food deliveries.

There is next to no electricity, gas or running water and some have been forced to eat grass and garden weeds.

Medical supplies have run out and hospitals are barely functioning amid daily shelling, drone threats and heavily mined roads.

The ceasefire is due to begin on Tuesday at 4am local time. It is unclear how long it will last.

News.title: Ed Miliband faction in Labour Party ‘waging war with Home Secretary’ after refusing to back immigration reforms
News.content:
Next

THE Ed Miliband faction in the Labour Party is waging war with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, insiders claim.

Ally Miatta Fahnbulleh sparked anger this week for refusing to back Labour’s immigration reforms.



The Energy Secretary eventually caved in by tweeting her support for the Home Secretary, but only after No10 told her to.

Weeks earlier, Foreign Secretary Mr Miliband appeared to cast doubt on the decision to ban Palestine Action.



One frontbencher said: “Miatta is seen as a loose cannon — and not a very good politician.”

A government insider said: “She’s only been an MP for two years but acts like she’s untouchable because she is close to Ed Miliband.



“It’s the Ed Miliband tendency. And it’ll only get worse.

“Ed and Miatta are wading into Home Office matters. He’s pushing for some kind of climbdown on proscribing [Palestine Action] as a terror group.”

Another senior Labour insider said: “Shabana is furious and a lot of the Cabinet are furious.

“Miatta’s veering all over the place. What has the Home Office got to do with her?”



In interviews, Ms Fahnbulleh failed to back Home Office plans to extend the time it takes an immigrant to get indefinite leave to remain.

Her spokesman declined to comment but pointed to her tweet, which read: “I fully support our Home Secretary and the Government’s position on migration reform.”

Asked about the Palestine Action comments, a source close to Mr Miliband said: “This is a matter for the Home Office, and the Foreign Secretary supports the Home Secretary in it.”

News.title: Twenty students aged five or below suspended from schools over sexual misconduct as shock figures hit record high in UK
News.content:
EDUCATION CRISIS Twenty students aged five or below suspended from schools over sexual misconduct as shock figures hit record high in UK







Next

TWENTY pupils aged five or below have been suspended from schools due to sexual misconduct, as shocking figures hit a record high.

In the 2024-2025 school year, 7,278 students were suspended for sexual misconduct, figures from the Department for Education show.



It’s the highest total since the current recoding method started in 2020.

Of those, 20 children aged five or under were suspended for sexual misconduct.



Nineteen of those were in the reception year.

Five kids in the infant years were expelled outright with no conditional return.



Primary schools accounted for 759 of all suspensions.

Suspensions due to sexual misconduct can cover sexual assaults, abuse, harassment and lewd behaviour.

This can be aimed at either other pupils or staff.

The latest figures show cases have risen by 12 per cent, from 6,479 in the previous school year.



The rise comes while the total number of suspensions for all other issues is dropping.

Ofsted, which inspects school, found sexual harassment was normalised among schoolchildren.

Teachers’ leaders have warned that misogynist online influencers, such as Andrew Tate, are shaping how boys treat girls in schools.

Pupils aged 13 and 14 were the most frequent offenders, accounting for 1,564 suspensions.

Schools can record up to three reasons for each suspension.



Amongst the worst cases, 143 pupils were permanently excluded from school last year.

Christopher McGovern, chairman of the Campaign for Real Education, said: “These shocking figures represent only the tip of the iceberg of misogyny in schools.

“Most cases go unreported.

“Schools are no longer safe places for girls and for female teachers.

“The Government needs to greatly expand the option of single-sex schooling rather than allowing it to largely disappear.”



Soma Sara, chief executive of the charity Everyone’s Invited, said: “We hope that schools are now more conscious of the reality of sexual harassment and abuse among children and young people, and are better equipped to identify it and intervene when it happens.

“For too long, the harm children were experiencing was not always being recognised or understood by the adults around them.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A government spokesman said: “As part of our strategy to halve violence against women and girls, we have pledged to make sure all young people are taught about healthy relationships and consent from an early age.

“We have also forced tech companies to tackle harmful content and protect young people online through the Online Safety Act.”

News.title: Three brothers face extradition to Poland over killing after fleeing to Britain before trial
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

KILLERS FACE BOOT Three brothers face extradition to Poland over killing after fleeing to Britain before trial







Next

THREE brothers face extradition in a British legal first after being jailed in their absence for a killing in their homeland.

The Polish trio were among thugs who battered and stomped on two men in the city of Radomsko in 2020.



One victim died days later after suffering a brain haemorrhage.

Dariusz Paczkowski, 30, Dawid Paczkowski, 29, and Hubert Paczkowski, 27, were charged with “participation in a beating resulting in the death of a person”.



They fled to Britain before a trial in Lodz last October, where each got five years.

Polish authorities issued arrest warrants and warehouse packer Dariusz, of Romford, Essex, and Hubert, of Southend, were nicked in June by National Extradition Unit officers.



Dawid was picked up in Southend last month.

The trio are now all in custody while facing extradition proceedings at Westminster Magistrates Court.



They are next due to appear on 30 October.

It is understood to be the first time in British legal history that three siblings have faced removal from the UK for crimes committed overseas.

The Crown Prosecution Service was unable to provide a record of any other similar case.

News.title: Wind-up radios flying off the shelves after Government urges Brits to prepare ‘three-day’ survival kit
News.content:
Next

IT seems panicking punters are on the same wavelength – after clearing the shelves of wind-up radios.

Shoppers have snapped up the retro gadget after the Government included it in a recommended survival kit for times of crisis.



Ministers say people should also have a battery-powered torch, sleeping bags and three days’ food and water stockpiled in case of bad weather, power blackouts, cybersecurity attacks or supply shortages.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting says people should be “alert but not alarmed”.



However, the rush to prepare for a national emergency has obliterated stocks of wind-up radios.

A Sun on Sunday sweep across 12 major stores in Newcastle on Friday found only a single outlet with any on the shelves.

Menkind was selling an emergency hand crank radio with torch and powerbank for £24.99.

But an assistant on the shop floor said: “I imagine they will go quickly.”

Elsewhere, high street shelves were bare, with wind-up models either out of stock or unavailable at the likes of Currys, John Lewis, Screwfix and Tesco.

Many online stores were the same. At Debenhams, the £36.95 Philips portable radio torch alarm has been cleared out, while the £25 InGenious emergency hand crank radio is out of stock at The Range.



Robert Dyas has no £56.99 travel radios with solar, hand crank and USB-C charging and Maplin is out of £18.99 IONOS Almere radios.

B&Q is among the few major names carrying a broad selection, online only. But many won’t arrive for up to ten days.

On Amazon, dispatch dates have slipped deep into next month, while bargain platform Temu has a hand crank radio with LED flashlight for just £10.96, but it requires minimum-spend basket add-ons and takes at least a week to arrive.

Consumer expert Martyn James said: “There’s no doubt the dire warning from the Government has prompted panic buying.

“High demand means companies are more likely to put up prices because they know they’ll sell them. But there’s no need to worry. The world isn’t going to end in the next week.”



Archivist Peter Daniels, 48, from Newcastle, was “shocked” by how hard it is to get a wind-up radio.

He said: “I assumed it would be easy as the Government was advising us to purchase them.

“I’ve been looking everywhere.”

Clever Trev’s brainwave to battle AIDS

TREVOR BAYLIS invented the wind-up radio in 1991 in a bid to help stop the spread of AIDS in Africa by educating rural listeners.



He was driven to act after watching a TV documentary about how the disease was taking hold on the continent, where a lack of electricity and high battery costs meant many had no access to informative broadcasts.

London-born Trevor set to work making a prototype.

His invention became known as the BayGen Freeplay: the world’s first self-powered, clockwork radio – which was manufactured in Cape Town and initially distributed through aid organisations.

Trevor, who died aged 80 in 2018, recalled: “Before the show was over, I was into my studio and I managed to get a bark of sound out of an instrument and that was, if you like, my eureka moment.”

The mechanism was powered by winding a folding lever on the radio casing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A network of gears allowed it to slowly unwind, spinning an internal dynamo generator and creating electricity to power the radio.



In 2015, Trevor was awarded a CBE for services to intellectual property.

Today, the humble clockwork radio remains a key piece of survival kit.

News.title: Mum who was part of first all-female terror plot sues jail chiefs after strip-search during hunt for smuggled phone
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

LAG SUES Mum who was part of first all-female terror plot sues jail chiefs after strip-search during hunt for smuggled phone







Next

A MUM who was part of Britain’s first all-female terror plot is suing justice bosses after she was strip-searched.

Prison officers checked Mina Dich while looking for a smuggled phone.



The 52-year-old was jailed in 2018 for helping her daughter Rizlaine Boular to plan an attack on cops in London.

Her other daughter, Safaa Boular, was convicted of plotting a ­grenade and gun attack on the British Museum.



Moroccan-born Dich, who wears a head-to-toe Jilbab gown, has brought a case under human rights laws, claiming she had “inhuman and degrading treatment”.

She is demanding £40,000 from Sodexo, which runs HMP Peterborough, over three searches in 2018 and 2019 — including the strip-search.



A phone was never found.

Cathryn McGahey KC, representing Sodexo, who operate the nick for the Ministry of Justice, told a court that the bar for degrading treatment “is not conceivably met”.

A justice source said: “It’s madness that inmates are able to bring ridiculous and expensive cases like this. But under existing laws, all that can be done is to fight them.”

Dich was understood to have been freed from jail to immigration detention in 2024.



We reported in April she had lost a bid to stay in the UK and was to be deported.

HMP Peterborough said it was unable to comment.

The case at Cambridge county court continues.

News.title: Two guilty of murder after man, 37, killed in terrifying broad daylight knife attack that sparked major police probe
News.content:
FATAL STABBING Two guilty of murder after man, 37, killed in terrifying broad daylight knife attack that sparked major police probe







Next

TWO people have been found guilty of murder after a man was stabbed to death in broad daylight, with the knife attack sparking a huge police investigation.

Danny Fowler, 37, was stabbed several times at around 5pm in Union Street, Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, on March 12.



He was pronounced dead at the scene and a large-scale investigation launched.

Ryan Townhill, 29, has now been found guilty of murder in a terrifying attack that lasted less than four minutes, following a six-week trial at Lincoln Crown Court.



Shannon Doocey, 31, was also found guilty of murder and possession of an offensive weapon.

The jury also found Martin Doocey guilty of manslaughter.

The pair were also involved in a separate altercation in Market Rasen in September 2025, which involved several multiple public order, violence and weapons offences – with those involved due to attend court for that incident on the day of Mr Fowler’s murder.

Shannon Doocey was found guilty of affray and possession of an offensive weapon in relation to the previous incident, while Martin Doocey was found guilty of possession of an offensive weapon.

All three are due to be sentenced on November 17.

The violence erupted in the centre of the town in full view of members of the public.



Ryan Townhill’s vehicle approached Mr Fowler’s vehicle when the altercation began.

Townhill delivered the first two blows and damaged the car’s tyres, the court heard.

Shannon Doocey left a nearby shop and joined the confrontation, armed with a broken wine bottle.

Mr Fowler moved towards Townhill and Shannon Doocey, armed with a baseball bat and was also seen with a knife.

As the altercation escalated, Mr Fowler fell to the ground and was stabbed several times.



Martin Doocey got involved in the altercation after Mr Fowler and fallen to the ground, the jury was told.

CCTV showed Townhill delivering nine blows with his knife, while Shannon Doocey carried out several blows, thought to be with the broken bottle.

Martin Doocey delivered 14 blows.

Shannon Doocey and Townhill then fled while Martin Doocey remained in Union Street.

CCTV footage showed him buying a bottle of whiskey and water in the area before he was arrested.



Detective Inspector Melissa Rooke, the senior investigating officer, said: “Danny Fowler lost his life in an act of extreme violence carried out in Market Rasen in the middle of the afternoon.

“What happened that day unfolded in a matter of seconds, but the consequences have been devastating and long-lasting for Danny’s family, those who witnessed the incident, and the wider community.

“This was an incident that took place in broad daylight in a busy town centre street, in full view of members of the public.

“A number of those witnesses have had to relive what they saw throughout this investigation and during the court process.

“The evidence presented to the jury included CCTV footage, forensic evidence and witness testimony, which enabled us to build a comprehensive picture of the events that led to Danny’s death.



“Our thoughts remain firmly with Danny’s family and loved ones.

“I would like to thank everyone who came forward with information during the investigation and throughout the subsequent court proceedings.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Their support has been invaluable in helping us establish the circumstances surrounding what happened.

“I would also like to recognise the dedication of the officers and staff involved in this investigation, alongside our partner agencies, whose professionalism ensured every available line of enquiry was pursued.”

News.title: Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters and use tear gas during unrest
News.content:
Police have clashed with protesters in Paris as some demonstrations in France turned violent on Saturday.

A largely peaceful day of protests turned into unrest after nightfall, as protesters were seen throwing objects and fireworks at police.

Around 70,000 officers were deployed across France for a second consecutive weekend and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.

The Interior Ministry estimated around 400,000 people took part in Saturday's demonstrations, with nearly 1,000 arrests made.

Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Paris, where he says there are few signs the unrest will ease soon.

News.title: Storm Boelo amber warnings kick in as parts of UK brace for 80mph gusts
News.content:
Amber weather warnings have come into force in Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England as Storm Boelo continues to move across the UK, with wind gusts up to 80mph forecast in the worst-hit areas.

Strong winds and heavy showers will intensify through Saturday night, with widespread gusts expected.

The amber warning for Scotland and England will stay in place until 21:00 on Sunday, bringing an increased risk of travel disruption and potential risk to life.

The second named storm in as many days comes as National Grid continues to restore power to thousands of properties in south-west England after the area was hit hardest by Storm Austen.

News.title: Met Police says letter with claims about Meghan's father not shared with other law enforcement
News.content:
Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.

He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having a leg amputated in 2025.

Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home, the Sun reported.

He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the FBI in July.

In a statement released by Meghan on Friday she said that when she received the information of the claims against her father she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".

Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Authorities in the Philippines have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father.

The BBC was told on Friday the matter was being investigated by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured his computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meghan is the only daughter of Markle and her mother Doria Ragland.

He pulled out of attending Meghan and Harry's wedding in 2018 - citing ill health - and they became estranged.

The duke and duchess moved to the US in 2020 after stepping down as working royals.

They returned to the UK with their children this year after six years away.

News.title: Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test
News.content:
But the widespread suggestion that you'll be able to blink and miss the Budget has got some hackles up in the Treasury. A budget, by its very nature, can never be a small event - it sets billions upon billions of taxes and spending decisions.

And there are likely to be extra taxes on banks, vows to sweep away some business regulation, particularly for small business, more powers passing to local leaders under the guise of devolution and more action on energy bills which are heading back up again.

John Healey has made it clear publicly and to staff, that he wants to encourage people with the guts and drive to start a business. One source said: "If you are taking on John's mantra about talking up Britain then you can't say, 'Nothing to see here'."

Whatever else the chancellor brings to Parliament in his red box, do not expect him to arrive with all the solutions to the country's very well-documented problems, whether that's getting the economy growing more convincingly, sorting out gaps in defence cash, welfare, social care, or new ways to pay off the country's groaning debts more quickly.

One former minister suggests even if Healey and Burnham had stumbled upon all the answers in a few months, it's just not possible to fix everything at the same time because of the constraints on the economy.

They wondered: "Is he going to invest in growth? Is he going to put everything he has into the challenges people will face this winter? Is he going to throw it at defence? There is just not enough to tackle all these problems simultaneously - ministers are going to be exposed to the cold light of day."

Burnham and Healey have to find a way of maintaining the balance in an unusually happy Labour Party.

MPs talk of ministers and Burnham himself being more visible and approachable in Parliament, knocking around with colleagues in the evening, fewer "golden slips" doled out when ministers were excused from voting alongside colleagues so they could get on with their important jobs.

One minister told me they'd had to tell their private office not to arrange for them to be "slipped" , from going to the Commons in the evening to see backbenchers.

It's paying off in the mood among MPs. One told me: "You're not feeling like the only way you can ever have a chat with a minister is by arranging an appointment for three months down the line â the soft touches really matter."

News.title: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep you and your home warmer for longer
News.content:
With the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in.

So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under Â£20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.

But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.

You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.

Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.

News.title: Strictly's new presenters - after mixed reviews have they found their feet?
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.

Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.

And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.

Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.

Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.

Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.

Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.

News.title: The artist dropping her debut album after a billion streams
News.content:
Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.

But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline.

"When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says.

"There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad.

"There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."

Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic.

"I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland.

"We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."

Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.

Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".

While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.

She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track".

"I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well.

"So there's a little message from me in each song."

News.title: How Brazil's changing working class is reshaping the presidential race
News.content:
In the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed SÃ£o Paulo's "Silicon Valley."

The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president.

Like many of Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried.

He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up.

"We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers.

"Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built."

The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics â even though FlÃ¡vio has faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies.

News.title: Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget
News.content:
The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.

It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.

Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost Â£8.9bn.

A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a Â£9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.

But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).

Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said that while hosting an Olympic Games would "likely provide a positive boost for the country", the cost of proposals would require "careful scrutiny".

He said the chancellor should use the Budget to bring down everyday costs before looking to "spend millions in taxpayer cash on reheated announcements made by his predecessor".

French added: "The irony is that Labour's new tourism tax will create a cost barrier for sports fans wanting to visit the North of England for an Olympic Games."

The new feasibility study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.

Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.

"Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."

News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport.

"We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement.

"Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

News.title: Murder charge after body found in wheelie bin
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder after a body was found partially within a wheelie bin, police have said.

Devon and Cornwall Police said Mohamed Abotaka, 36, of Grand Parade, Plymouth, was charged with the murder of 52-year-old Ali Barzai. The force said Abotaka was due to appear in court on Monday.

Police said Barzai's body was found in a service lane off Grand Parade at about 06:40 BST on Wednesday.

Det Insp Chris Lithgow urged people not to speculate and said a heightened police presence would remain in the area in the coming days.

News.title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of tour
News.content:
Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.

The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.

While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.

The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs".

Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.

But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices.

"They're getting changed," he said on Instagram.

"It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."

The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front.

"The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it," Fender said.

"I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs... it won't be happening on this tour."

He is not the first musician to raise concerns over ticket pricing.

Zara Larsson agreed with fans earlier this year that her tickets were too expensive.

The Swedish singer said while she did not have control over the prices, she hoped she would in the future.

News.title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?
News.content:
But none of that helps to verify the claim to the title of England's oldest pub - so what does?

Wright said, put simply, none of the other pubs possessed the archaeological evidence, archival references or scientific data "to actually back up the claims".

He said: "It's all about carefully placing all of the evidence together and working out in what order the real claimants go - and The George came out with the crown."

Pub historian Charo Havermans agreed with that assertion.

"The strongest claims are when the history meets the science," she said.

"For example, tree ring dating can give us an idea of how old the timber or the wood used is.

"What we know about those times is that people wouldn't dilly dally so if they've cut down a tree, they're going to use it then," Havermans said.

"It's a pretty accurate way of knowing when the building materials were used to create that structure."

Havermans also said historical records such as licensing data, local maps, or the Domesday Book could help date a pub.

However, we may never truly know where the oldest boozers are - a sentiment reinforced by Guinness World Records which has "rested" the accolade for the oldest pub since 2000, "when it became clear that it was not possible to verify it in full".

A spokeswoman for Guinness World Records said it was "never able to state definitively which was the oldest pub in the country, since the age and historical usage of buildings is, in many cases, uncertain".

News.title: Thousands of people gather in support of Drumcree Orangemen
News.content:
The first part of the parade was followed by a series of speeches, mainly from members of the Orange Order.

This was very much an Orange Order event and not a political rally but inevitably there was a political tone to many of the comments.

There was explicit criticism of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher, the secretary of state and the first minister, but also implicit criticism of the leaders of the two biggest unionist parties - the DUP and Ulster Unionist Party.

Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister was applauded but by far the loudest cheers were for the Orange Order's legal adviser Jamie Bryson and the local MP Lockhart.

She was invited on to the stage and presented with a special gift for her support of the Orangemen.

Lockhart was the only politician to take to the stage, where she repeated her challenge to the DUP leadership: "Profound consequences must mean profound consequences. Michelle O'Neill must go.

"That's where I stand, and this lady is not for turning."

Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson warned politicians that they could face consequences at the next election over the Drumcree dispute.

"Politicians need to remember that we put them into office and we can take them out of office," he said.

He added that the Orange Order had won the right "to return home via our traditional route and Portadown District intends to exercise that right on a date and time of our choosing, and if necessary, without further recourse".

Orange Order Deputy District Master Alistair Power said Drumcree must not be allowed to divide unionism.

"It should not be used by parties to attack each other publicly over differences of opinion," he added. "We need to stand united."

News.title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding
News.content:
More than Â£1m is to be spent on nature recovery projects, including the restoration of habitats destroyed by a fire which ripped through a huge area of hillside in the Cairngorms.

The Scottish government funding will support habitat, species and river restoration, control of invasive non-native species and deer management across Scotland.

It includes Â£150,100 for recovery and nature restoration work following the Abernethy wildfire in the Cairngorms in July, to restore damaged habitats, help wildlife recover and reduce the risk of future wildfires.

News.title: Reward offered over murder in flat used as brothel
News.content:
A Â£20,000 reward is being offered by Crimestoppers in connection with the murder of a man who was found dead in a Birmingham flat in 2022.

Jinming Zhang had been stabbed multiple times before he was found in the property, which police said was being used as a brothel, in Moseley Street in Digbeth.

West Midlands Police previously released CCTV of a suspect, while a DNA sample from the suspected killer found at the scene did not produce a match on the national database.

The case was featured in the BBC series of Forensics: The Real CSI last year, which revealed police believed the murder suspect may have sustained a hand injury in the frenzied attack.

Jenny Birch, who has been overseeing the investigation, urged anyone with information "no matter how small" to contact police.

"Someone out there knows something, and we won't give up until we have answers," she said.

News.title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
News.content:
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.

As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit Â£100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.

The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.

"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.

"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.

"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."

The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.

"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.

"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."

The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing Â£200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.

News.title: British and French paratroopers in largest airborne drill for decades amid Russia fears
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thousands of service members from Britain and France have joined forces in a military wargame intended to demonstrate the defence of Nato territory against potential foreign aggression.

The drills featured a major airborne operation, among the largest conducted in two decades, with British and French paratroopers leaping from RAF transport aircraft over German soil.

The joint drills come amid heightened security fears across Europe driven by Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, as Russian troops probe Nato frontiers and the Kremlin faces accusations of directing arson, sabotage, and assassinations within European countries.

Conducted at the Sennelager military training area in Germany, Exercise Rhino Titan pushed the UK’s 16 Air Assault Brigade to respond to adversaries armed with electronic warfare systems and drone fleets, reflecting the tactical capabilities Russia is anticipated to employ.

RAF A400M Atlas aircraft ( CPL Tim Laurence RAF/MoD/Crown Copyright/PA Wire )

Overall, roughly 2,500 personnel took part, which included 600 French and British paratroopers dropping from four RAF A400M Atlas aircraft.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "The threats we face in the 21st century require an updated, modern approach to warfare – and our adaptable armed forces are preparing accordingly.

"Alongside our French and German allies, this large-scale training exercise shows we can deliver rapid, large-scale airborne power anywhere it’s needed to defend Nato territory.

"This combination of troops and specialised equipment is what is required to deter our adversaries and keep Britain and our allies safe."

Brigadier Ed Cartwright, commander of 16 Air Assault Brigade, said: "We have been given a realistic challenge to defend Nato territory and pitted against an enemy using drones and electronic warfare, which is what we would face on the modern battlefield."

News.title: MAGA candidate reveals how he feels about Trump constantly talking about his rear
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Ohio senator who has been the subject of President Donald Trump’s constant praise for his physique has revealed how he feels about the comments.

Twice in recent days, Trump took time during rally speeches to talk about Republican Jon Husted’s “ass.” While appearing Saturday on Fox News, Husted was asked about his reaction to Trump’s comments.

“Well, I have to tell you, when I woke up the next morning after hearing that, I told my wife, I’m like, ‘Hey, I think I got to get down to the gym and keep up my reputation! So, I gotta keep working out,'” Husted said.

The Republican in a tight race added that he is part of an athletic family, as he played college football and his wife runs marathons.

“Well, it got you a lot of headlines. Maybe some that you didn’t expect, but certainly a lot of press,” Fox host Aishah Hasnie quipped.

Ohio Sen. Jon Husted has revealed how he feels about President Donald Trump talking about his body ( Getty Images )

At rallies in North Carolina and Ohio, Trump talked about Husted’s body.

“But I looked at his ass, and then I looked at his legs,” Trump said. “I said, ‘His ass, s***, it’s like, it’s like a pile of muscle. Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. He’s like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster!’”

Trump comments were mocked both online and by TV pundits. CNN’s Anderson Cooper ran a montage of the president talking about other officials’ bodies during one show this week.

The clips included several politicians. At one point, it showed Trump calling Georgia Republican lieutenant gubernatorial nominee Greg Dolezal a “good-looking guy.”

“You’re not allowed to say that about women or men anymore. It’s the end of your political career. But he is a good-looking guy,” Trump said.

Cooper then ended with a quip of his own about Husted and Trump’s comments.

“As for Senator Husted, his ass may be hard, but his polling is soft. According to the latest CNN poll of polls, he’s down five points,” Cooper said.

Husted is running against Democrat Sherrod Brown in a competitive Ohio race. A Cook Political Report poll released this week found Brown up on Husted, 49 percent to 43 percent.

News.title: Why was Cole Palmer sent off against Tottenham?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Cole Palmer was sent off as Chelsea experienced a late capitulation to suffer their first home defeat to Tottenham since 2018.

The Blues fell behind in the 78th minute when 21-year-old goalkeeping understudy Mike Penders, making his full Premier League debut in the absence of the injured Emi Martinez, punched into his own net from a corner in the 78th minute.

Things then went from bad to worse for Xabi Alonso’s side in the pouring rain, with Blues talisman Palmer catching former team-mate and Chelsea youth product Conor Gallagher as he brought down a Spurs free-kick.

Palmer’s studs caught the ankle of the midfielder, who had replaced James Maddison after he suffered another gut-wrenching injury setback in a Tottenham shirt.

open image in gallery Cole Palmer leaves the field after being sent off against Tottenham ( Getty )

Palmer and Chelsea players vigorously appealed for the decision to be overturned, which VAR does now have the power to do with second yellow cards.

But Chris Kavanagh stuck with his decision and Chelsea were reduced to 10 men.

Palmer will now miss Chelsea’s trip to Liverpool for the Carabao Cup.

Palmer picked up his first yellow in similarly-dramatic circumstances, barging into a kneeled Mateus Fernandes with his torso after the Portuguese midfielder committed a cynical foul, pawing the bawl away while downed to stop Chelsea charging on goal.

A scuffle ensued which saw Fernandes and Micky van de Ven also booked. Roberto De Zerbi said after the match that he thought Palmer should have been sent off for this incident alone.

Speaking on the first caution and Palmer’s eventual sending off, Alonso said: “I haven't seen them on TV but as far as I have been told that probably he [the referee] got it right, so for sure for Cole but for everyone.

“We think [up until] now we haven't received any red card and we need to continue that way because we need to have this maturity to deal with difficult moments, when you have conceded 1-0, still probably was 15-20 minutes to go, so we have to be on the way. I need to check the action to talk with Cole but it is one to learn for the future for sure.”

Tottenham put the seal on a 2-0 victory seven minutes after Palmer’s dismissal, with Mathys Tel finishing off a superb individual goal to wrap up Spurs’ first triumph on Chelsea soil 2018.
