World.title: U.S. birth rate drops to record low, but older women are having more babies
World.content:
U.S. birth rate drops to record low, but older women are having more babies

toggle caption i CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP

Sarah Harris was 36 years old when she gave birth to her daughter Bridget last year. She describes motherhood as equal parts joy and exhaustion. "When you have a baby in your mid-30s, what you gain in wisdom and experience you also lose in terms of energy," Harris says with a laugh.

Harris, who lives in Vermont, was laid off from a job four months after Bridget was born. She says she's still figuring out what her career and her life will look like with a child. Harris thinks a lot of women are like her. They're wrestling with financial uncertainty and waiting much later to choose pregnancy.

Sponsor Message

There's also the high cost of raising a child, which Harris said convinced her that one is enough. "I think in another era or another life or another scenario, I might have had more children," Harris says. "I think we're in a difficult societal moment and so that's absolutely affecting people's reproductive choices."

Harris is, in fact, part of a slow revolution in what motherhood and parenting look like in the United States The latest report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found the general fertility rate for women fell by 1% to a new record low in 2025. That continues a two-decade trend toward fewer children.

Steep drops in parenting among U.S. women in their 20s

The one-year drop for 20-somethings was even more eye-catching. "Certainly the 6% decline in the birthrate for women age 20 to 24 is noteworthy," said Brady Hamilton, a demographer at the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics who co-authored the report. He noted that women in their late teens also saw a 7% decline.

A separate study released last month by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta found Gen Z women, in their late teens and twenties, "are dramatically less likely to want children" compared with U.S. women of previous generations.

Sponsor Message

"Several factors have been identified as contributing to this lower desire to have children, such as increased labor market opportunities and agency among women, rising financial costs, changing priorities, and [concerns about] maternal mortality," the study found.

Dr. Tanise Branche, medical director of labor and delivery at Temple Health, a health, research and training network in Philadelphia, told NPR more of her younger women patients are following a different life script.

"They're starting to focus not necessarily just on what they can bring to kids, but what's going to be best for them," she says.

Women in their 30s and 40s saw "significant" birthrate increase

Meanwhile, the latest CDC data shows a small but significant increase in older women, ages 30 to 45, who are choosing to become pregnant.

Branche says more women, including herself, are building careers and stable lives before becoming mothers.

Branche is currently pregnant with her fourth child. "I will be 43 with my last delivery and I started this reproductive journey at 37," she said. "I see the net positive being that we have a choice."

Fewer children because of choice — and affordability

As a consequence of this shift, there are fewer children now in the U.S. The population under age 18 is falling steadily, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, dropping by more than 1 million from 2010 to 2020.

Some experts also believe women would choose to have more kids if they could afford them and had proper supports that include affordable housing, daycare and health insurance.

"The fact that there are a lot of people who still say they want families, but don't feel like they're able to have them [is a concern]," says Anna Louie Sussman, author of a new book on parenting choices called Inconceivable. "Young people say, I can barely take care of myself I can't imagine taking care of someone else."

Sussman herself is part of the trend toward delayed motherhood. Because of her own concerns about affordability and her career, she froze her eggs and waited to have her child until she was in her early 40s.

Sponsor Message

"I do feel lucky that I'm a little further along professionally than I would have been in my 20s or even 30s," she said.

As women build different lives and birthrates keep falling, the U.S. is changing. The median age is rising rapidly, reaching 39.4 years old in 2025. More states, including Vermont where Sarah Harris lives, are seeing actual population decline, according to the Census Bureau.

"I think about it a lot because I live in a very small place where we're hoping to keep the doors of our elementary school open for as long as we can," she says.

World.title: This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm
World.content:
This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

Given all that's happened in American politics since 2019, it may be hard to believe there's been anything missing.

But the decade of the 2020s has yet to see a midterm that mattered much — or that ranked among the impact midterms of past decades.

That sets the 2020s apart, as every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.

These big-impact midterms have also shifted power in the statehouses, often signaling changes in state and national political landscapes that have mattered and lasted.

Midterms do not attract the same level of voter participation or voter interest as presidential elections. When the White House is not at stake, "low propensity voters" tend to tune out. Overall vote totals slide by about one-third.

Sponsor Message

But those voters who show up for midterms elect just as many members of Congress and fill just as many state legislative seats as voters in presidential years. Moreover, midterm voters determine about two-thirds of the nation's governorships.

The big midterms have tended to come in presidents' second terms, when their popularity and political energy may be waning. And just because a president is not on the ballot does not mean he's irrelevant. Historically, each president's detractors have seen midterms as an opportunity, while his supporters have often been complacent — or at least less motivated.

All this contributes to the general expectation that the midterms arriving Nov. 3 will be important, and perhaps momentous.

Flexing midterm muscles

Because this is a decade with three presidential cycles (2020, 2024 and 2028), it is also a decade with just two midterms. One went by in 2022. Some expected at the time that a "big red wave" would sweep then-President Biden's majorities out of Congress.

It did not happen. Democrats held on in the Senate, and the House shifted from barely Democratic to barely Republican. That did bring an end to House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's second (and last) turn with the Big Gavel. But the GOP would spend much of the next two years struggling to unite behind a speaker of their own.

Sponsor Message

That's a far cry from the big midterms that have at times rivaled presidential elections for responding to the mood of the times and rearranging the landscape.

If we take the last hundred years as our sample, we can start with the midterms that followed the Wall Street "Crash of 1929." That financial panic set off a sequence of events that would be called the Great Depression, and the collateral damage included the closing of an era of Republican dominance in Washington.

That era ended with the midterms of 1930, which cost the GOP eight Senate seats and 52 seats in the House in November 1930. Although the GOP initially retained small majorities in both chambers, they lost it in the House with the results of a few special elections early in 1931.

toggle caption i National Archives

The Senate remained nominally Republican but featured a working majority of Democrats and progressive Republicans. A page had been turned, and Democrats would take control outright in 1932 and hold that majority through World War II.

After that war had ended, the period of Democratic hegemony under President Franklin Roosevelt also ended, and abruptly, with the results of the midterm of 1946.

Pendulum swings both ways

Republican numbers in Congress had fallen so far in the FDR years ( below 100 at one point in the 435-seat House ) that it seemed impossible for them to return to power. But in 1946 they stormed back to majority control of both House and Senate in a single midterm cycle.

Midterms have continued to serve as political regulators in the generations since. Dwight Eisenhower won two landslide elections as president in the 1950s, but he lost the House in 1954 and needed the vice president to break ties in the Senate.

In his second term, the re-elected "Ike" did not control Capitol Hill, and in the 1958 midterms saw his party drop to just 35 seats in the Senate .

Sponsor Message

The Senate Democrats first elected in 1958 established a critical mass that would later drive the bipartisan super-majorities needed to break the filibuster and pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

In the same era, Democrats in Congress enacted a raft of social programs that would become part of the language, such as Medicare and Medicaid. It was all part of President Lyndon Johnson's "Great Society" program.

What goes up …

toggle caption i AFP via Getty Images/AFP

But by the midterm year of 1966, much of the energy from LBJ's landslide election in 1964 had been expended — and much more had been siphoned off by his escalation of the war in Vietnam.

Right on time, the midterm arrived, and while the Democrats only took a haircut in the Senate elections they lost a painful 47 seats to the GOP in the House. It gave the party a new lease on life and encouraged its new emphasis on winning in the South . The redirection would guide the party's 1968 presidential candidate, Richard Nixon, and remain a focus for the onetime "Party of Lincoln" for decades to come.

Also in the midterm of 1966, out on the West Coast, a first-time candidate named Ronald Reagan won the governorship of California. People were starting to use the term "Sunbelt."

Yet another midterm correction

But what the midterms of 1966 gave the GOP, the midterms of 1974 would largely take away. Nixon had been elected president in 1968, pursuing what was called a Southern Strategy, and was reelected in a resounding 49-state landslide in 1972.

But by 1974 it had all gone the other way for Nixon. The "Watergate" scandals emerged from his 1972 campaign's use of burglary and electronic surveillance among other unsavory tactics. An attempt to cover it all up blew back on the White House and forced Nixon to resign on the brink of impeachment in August of 1974 – just three months before the midterm for his second term.

Sponsor Message

The result was a crushing defeat for the GOP, the loss of 48 seats in the House and several more in the Senate (where the Democrats already had more than 60 votes).

While it is tempting to attribute these losses to Nixon's downfall, the country had — to some extent — rallied behind his vice president and successor, Gerald R. Ford. The underlying vulnerability of the GOP was the state of the economy, which was suffering from inflation and the hangover from the oil embargo of 1973 by Arab members of OPEC, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

That embargo, a side effect of the Arab-Israeli "Yom Kippur War" of 1973, temporarily raised the price of crude oil from $3 to $12 and introduced Americans to the phrases "oil shock" and "energy crisis."

Reagan rises and falls

toggle caption i Consolidated News Pictures/AFP via Getty Images

Reagan became the dominant political personality of the 1980s, defeating incumbent President Jimmy Carter in 1980 and winning a 49-state landslide reelection in 1984. He was able to carry in a majority for Republicans in the Senate and establish a kind of working majority in the House with the aid of conservative Democrats in that chamber.

On the strength of those elections, restrained only marginally by the midterm elections of 1982, Reagan began his second term on top of the world. But he soon learned how hard that height can be to hold. As he neared his second midterm, Democrats were on the march nationally and restoring their strength in the more populous Southern states.

In 1986, Democrats defeated six GOP senators who had been elected with Reagan in 1980. The net gain of eight Senate seats gave them a 55-45 majority. In the session of Congress that followed, the Senate would override Reagan's veto of a highway bill and reject his nomination of Robert Bork to the Supreme Court. Reagan was a spent force.

Yet more dramatic reversals to come

Reagan was able to see his vice president, George H.W. Bush, take the White House in 1988, but the party's hopes for momentum into the 1990 midterms were largely unfulfilled. The presidency was also lost in 1992, when Democrat Bill Clinton won a three-way race with just 43% of the popular vote, defeating Bush and independent candidate H. Ross Perot.

Sponsor Message

Clinton's lack of a majority and list of frustrations in his first term set the stage for a bruising first midterm election in 1994. But what came was beyond bruising. Republicans stormed to their first majority in the House (54 seats net) in 40 years and recaptured the Senate with eight new seats there as well.

The new GOP speaker, Newt Gingrich of Georgia, was a hard-driving partisan who had portrayed the chamber as a House of Ill Repute, the title of a book he and other House Republicans had published.

The use of a "Contract with America" theme promised lower taxes, less corruption and a healthier economy in a compact agenda that had voter appeal as well.

Gingrich explicitly rejected the go-along-get-along attitude of previous GOP leaders in the House and advocated confrontation. The strategy proved less fruitful once he had the Big Gavel, however, and Gingrich spent much of his time as speaker making deals with Clinton. Internal dissatisfaction with him forced him out late in 1998.

Mood swings in the 2000s

In the new century that followed, parties have continued to prosper when their presidential candidates win and give ground in the midterms. George W. Bush was an exception as the president after the terror attacks of September 2001. In his first midterm the following year, the GOP made gains across the board.

But the larger dynamic caught up to him in 2006, when he and his party took what he called "a thumpin'" in elections at all levels. Bush had initially gained popularity with his "War on Terror" and won a second term. But thereafter, his invasion of Iraq had become an albatross. And in 2006 he paid the historic price, losing both his party majorities in the House and Senate. The new majority in the House made Pelosi the first woman speaker in history.

Sponsor Message

That created an atmosphere of optimism for Democrats, who elected Barack Obama president in 2008 and gave him majorities in the House and Senate (the latter briefly reaching 60 seats). But Obama felt the sting of the midterms early — much as Clinton had. Republicans in 2010 capitalized on an economy still experiencing the recession that had aided Obama's win in 2008. The GOP also capitalized on fears and confusion surrounding the enactment of the Affordable Care Act, or "Obamacare," in 2010.

Echoing his predecessor, Obama called this setback "a shellacking," and settled in to work with a much diminished Senate majority and a Republican-dominated House under Speaker John Boehner.

toggle caption i Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

Obama managed to thread the needle well enough to win a second term for himself in 2012, but the House remained Republican and the Senate followed suit in Obama's second midterm election in 2014.

That second midterm revealed continuing GOP strength across the South and Midwest and to some degree augured the Electoral College majorities that would make Donald J. Trump president in 2016 and 2024.

If the 2020s are to have a midterm with the kind of impact others have had, roughly once a decade for a century, the last opportunity for that to happen is Nov. 3.

If the once-a-decade rhythm has any rationale, in fact, the pressure for a meaningful midterm ought to be building substantially. And in fact most pollsters, pundits and other prognosticators now predict Democrats could flip control of the House and even the Senate as well.

Just as in the previous 10 cycles, the current cycle combines economic concerns (including energy prices) and negative stories about incumbents in various offices. It is the party perceived as being in power that is exposed in a midterm, and it pays a price when voters perceive that party to have lost its mandate — or at least its momentum.

World.title: Convicted murderer who attended McGill's faculty of law now back in custody
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A convicted murderer who has stirred controversy while attending law courses at McGill University is back in custody while authorities look more closely at his case.

The Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) confirmed to CBC News on Saturday that a suspension warrant for Jeffrey George Ewert was issued.

“The offender has returned to custody while a more thorough assessment of the situation is being conducted,” the statement said. Two sources had confirmed to CBC that Ewert had been picked up on Friday.

Ewert was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder for attacks against two women in B.C. in 1984 and is serving a life sentence.

He was granted day parole in 2025 and began taking law classes and going to faculty events at the Montreal institution in August. He had not been on campus since early October, according to a statement from McGill's provost.

His parole was extended for another six months in June 2026. While various clinical assessments ranked Ewert’s risk of reoffending as moderate to high, official parole documents say with close supervision at a halfway house and clinical follow-up, that risk “seems to fall more into the moderate risk category.”

The parole board did express concern about his interactions with and attitudes toward women.

In a statement Saturday, the federal agency that oversees adult offenders said a conditional release can be suspended in situations where there are “reasonable grounds to believe that the offender has breached a condition of release or that the risk they present can no longer be safely managed in the community.”

The case will be reviewed with the established post-release decision-making process, the agency said. That could include further consideration by the Parole Board of Canada (PBC).

The CSC says given it is an active case, it can’t comment further or provide further information about what led to the suspension as per the Privacy Act.

Presence stirs debate at McGill

But his attending McGill has created a deep divide over the presence of a convicted killer in the classroom.

One petition has circulated outlining why students feel unsafe and don’t want to be in Ewert’s presence. The petition expressed concern over his alleged behaviour while attending McGill.

However, another petition argued that excluding Ewert from campus undermines his access to education and rehabilitation as an Indigenous man and a survivor of the Sixties Scoop.

The CSC says information about an offender's time in the community is continually gathered.

“When concerns arise regarding an offender's behaviour, compliance with release conditions, or ability to be safely managed in the community, CSC takes appropriate action,” the CSC said.

“If the risk can no longer be safely managed in the community, CSC may suspend the offender's release and return them to custody. CSC works closely with its partners to respond quickly when circumstances require intervention.”

In a statement to CBC on Friday, a spokesperson for McGill said the "safety and security of our students is paramount."

The university also promised to "actively review its admissions processes to ensure a similar situation never happens again."

World.title: Musk says he was behind Starlink speed restriction in Ukraine
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia.

Musk's admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.

Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defence against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.

After Ukraine said the services had been restored, Musk spoke out on the speed restrictions that began last week. In a post Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service.

WATCH | Carney 'concerned' about Starlink slowdown: Carney says he is 'concerned' about reported Starlink slowdown in Ukraine | Duration closed caption 3:10 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he is concerned about the reported slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink satellite system in Ukraine, which created 'real consequences.' He says Canadians likewise 'do not want to be caught in a situation where we are reliant on one provider that may change their view' and compromise Canadian sovereignty.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine's defences since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

The restoration follows a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.

Restriction sparked Ukraine, U.S. tension

The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by U.S. President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."

Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. U.S. Vice-President JD Vance has hinted at White House co-ordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement.

Russia, Ukraine continue strikes

Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said Saturday.

Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks.

Ukraine's General Staff said Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city.

Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday's attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.

Ukrainian drones also reached Russia's Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometres from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said drones "reached a northern industrial hub."

Online retailer Ozon said Saturday that its logistics centre in Omsk has been attacked by a drone, but there were no casualties. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted.

World.title: Voters head to the polls for B.C. provincial election
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

British Columbians are heading to the polls on Saturday to elect their next provincial government.

The snap provincial election was called last month, with more than 350 candidates running across 93 ridings.

Polling stations are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. PT on Saturday.

People were seen braving the rain at a polling station in Coquitlam Saturday morning.

Among them, Michelle Stone. She says despite having two elections within a week of each other, she says she was able to do research and make an informed decision.

"It's pretty confusing, it's so many people to vote for," she said. "It was tough to have both around the same time."

As a parent of two children, she says affordability and cost of living for families is top of mind.

For Barb Dumont, who also cast her ballot on Saturday morning, health and Indigenous rights were important election issues.

"We want health for seniors to be a big priority," she said.

"I also think Indigenous rights are very important.... It's been neglected for far too long."

To be eligible to cast a ballot, voters must be at least 18 years old on Oct. 24 and a Canadian citizen who has resided in B.C. since April 23, 2026.

Many voters will have received a voter information card with details on where they can cast their ballot.

Elections B.C. has provided an application for voters to find their nearest voting place.

The provincial elections office has a list of acceptable ID documents that voters would need to prove their identity and residential address when voting. Voters who don't have the required identification can have their identity vouched for by a person who meets specific eligibility requirements.

Anyone who hasn't registered can still do so in person on election day.

Volunteers from Apathy is Boring hit the streets of downtown Vancouver Saturday, encouraging people to vote. (Ivan De Jacquelin/CBC)

Volunteers from non-partisan nonprofit Apathy is Boring hit the streets of downtown Vancouver Saturday, with hopes to engage people and encourage them to make it to the polls.

Director Erika De Torres says they are particularly trying to reach young voters.

"What we've found time and time again, across all different levels of government, is that young people don’t necessarily show up as much as their different intergenerational counterparts," she said.

And with two elections in one week, De Torres says the group is there to help provide information on the different levels of government and what they do.

"Please go out and vote, you have until 8 p.m. to go show elected politicians, candidates that you care," she said.

CBC News will bring you up-to-the-minute coverage after polls close, with a live election special starting at 7:30 p.m. PT.

Hosts Gloria Macarenko and Jason D’Souza will host B.C. Votes 2026, a special evening of election programming featuring guest interviews and in-depth analysis and broadcast coverage available in ASL across all CBC B.C. platforms.

Where to watch and listen:

Online: Live streaming on CBC News BC , CBC Gem , cbc.ca/bc as well as on YouTube .

TV: Live on CBC Television (check your TV service provider for channel).

World.title: From horses to electric cars: Sask. couple sees world transform over 75-year marriage
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Larry and Helen Frey figure no one else had a wedding night quite like theirs.

On that chilly November night in 1951, they came home to a rugged prairie house with no cupboards or electricity.

"We had to take our bed apart, bring it out where this cookstove was. You light a fire and get everything warmed up," said Larry, who's now 96. "That's how tough life was."

Their love and sense of humour is still burning strong 75 years later. Helen, 97, has a big chuckle recalling that frosty wedding night.

"I thought it was great," she laughs.

"Nobody has that story to tell, [that] they had to take their bed apart and put it beside the kitchen stove before they could have sex that night. What the heck!"

Life's challenges clearly did not deter the. The Freys are now celebrating a huge milestone at their home in Fort Qu'Appelle, Sask.: a wedding anniversary marking three-quarters of a century together.

Helen, left, and Larry Frey remember having to do everything for themselves: growing their own food, building their own barn and home, and farming to make their living. (Submitted by Cheryl Lendvoy)

They've seen huge changes in the world, from farming with horses and having no phones to zipping across the country in an electric car and Facetiming their children on cell phones.

They first met when he was 21 and she was 22.

"I married an older woman because I was told they were more fun," Larry jokes.

Helen was working as a clerk at a store when she made up her mind about getting to know Larry. They hadn't even met at that point, but she'd heard he was a caring man, she says.

"So when I first saw him walk in the store, I thought, 'Oh my God, I chose him, and how funny-looking he is and how young he is.'"

Larry says he noticed her figure immediately.

"She still looks the same," he adds.

Biggest changes in their lifetime

Farming was hard work. Larry says things changed drastically over the years, from using literal horse power with a team of horses and threshing machines, to using high-powered machines.

He's always been crazy about cars, and even now, he still picks the best. Larry's eyes grow big with excitement when he talks about driving his electric car.

Larry and Helen Frey in their electric vehicle on a Saskatchewan highway. (Submitted by Cheryl Lendvoy)

Growing up, there were hardly any paved roads. For their early dates, the couple often went on horseback.

Electricity made the biggest change in their lifetime.

"[You] didn't have to go down the cellar to get something to eat," Larry recalls. "A refrigerator, a block heater on a car. You didn't have to light a fire under the damn thing. These were big changes."

Another big change was in the people around them: four children, 10 grandkids, 16 great-grandkids and even one great-great-grandchild. Family and friends will all join them this month to celebrate their exciting milestone.

Larry and Helen Frey on their wedding day 75 years ago. (Submitted by Cheryl Lendvoy)

Do they have tips on how to stay happily married?

Larry's advice is short and to the point: "Button your lip."

Sometimes the best thing in a relationship is to give your partner space, he says.

Helen says she isn't qualified to give advice.

"The years just go by and you keep on living life," she says, noting that over the course of their relationship, they've shared amazing moments of joy but also hardships and tragedy. They've met all of it together.

"Live every day as you find it," she says, looking over to her husband.

"I just look at him and think, 'Oh God, he's mine.' And I'm so thankful."

World.title: 'They’re the nicest people': Obama mocks Trump for hitting Canada with tariffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former U.S. president Barack Obama, who delivered a lengthy speech Saturday at a campaign event for Democratic candidates in Ohio, took a moment to call out President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada. 'They're like our ... friendly neighbours to the north and he's ... picking a fight with them?

Obama mocks Trump over trade war with 'the people who gave us maple syrup'

Former U.S. president Barack Obama slammed the Trump administration's tariff regime on Saturday, and mocked the absurdity of engaging in a trade war with long-time ally Canada.

"The big trade war he's starting now is with that well-known evil empire: Canada," Obama said at a Cleveland rally for Democratic candidates in Ohio.

"These are the people who gave us maple syrup and Martin Short.… They're the nicest people," he joked. "They're our friendly neighbours to the north, and he's picking a fight with them?"

Obama, who has been stumping for Democrats ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, also criticized Donald Trump's tariffs policy more generally, saying they have had the expected negative effect on U.S. consumers who bear the brunt of the rising costs.

Those rising costs have hampered Republican chances in the midterms, especially in border states, leading Trump to announce on Friday that he plans to lift tariffs on some Canadian products.

WATCH | Trump to lift some tariffs on Canada before U.S. midterms: Trump to lift some tariffs on Canada before U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:41 Ahead of the U.S. midterms, the Trump Administration is lifting 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian products but adding them to others. The President also suggested a trade deal may be close, but Prime Minister Mark Carney was more cautious.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said on CBC's Power & Politics that Ottawa isn't expecting a deal before before the Nov. 3 vote.

The U.S. and Canada have been engaging in retaliatory tariffs since Trump first launched his levy campaign last year — ostensibly to combat alleged fentanyl trafficking and trade imbalances — and trade talks broke down in August.

Trump repeated lashes at Canada

Trump has routinely used Canada as a punching bag in his campaign rally speeches.

"At some point, we're making a deal that's gonna be amazing," Trump said during a stop in Highland Heights, Ky., on Oct. 17.

"But for years we've lost billions and billions of dollars, and they just felt so emboldened."

He was cheered when he called former prime minister Justin Trudeau a "loser" before taking aim at his successor, Mark Carney.

"Your current guy's good … he's a nice guy, but he's not nice when it comes to trade," he said.

"They're learning and they're suffering."

World.title: Toronto police seeking mother, 22, for allegedly abducting her 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto police are seeking the public’s help in locating three missing children, allegedly abducted by their mother from the Midland Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East area.

Daniel, 6, Irina, 3, and four-month-old Anastasia were having a semi-supervised visit with a relative on Friday, when their mother took them and fled the premises, police said Saturday.

Their mother, Somerda Miclescu, 22, is believed to be driving a 2017 White Ford Expedition SUV with Ontario licence plate DJJS 875, according to police.

From left, Daniel, 6, Irina, 3, and four-month-old Anastasia were having a semi-supervised visit with a relative on Friday, when their mother took them and fled the premises, police say. (Toronto Police Service)

The mother does not have legal custody of the children and her location is unknown, police said.

Police described her as 5-7, around 180 pounds, with long, dark black hair. Police say she was last seen wearing a long black skirt and a dark-coloured top.

Police had first responded to a call on Friday at around 11:30 a.m. for an abduction in the Midland Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East area.

Ionut Stroe, 25, is also wanted as a person of interest for owning the vehicle Miclescu fled in.

Unrelated to the alleged abduction, police say Stroe is currently wanted for four counts of failing to comply with a release order.

Police described him as being around 5-11, 235 pounds, with a tattoo on his right forearm.

Ionut Stroe, 25, is also wanted by police as a person of interest for owning the vehicle Somerda Miclescu fled in. (Toronto Police Service)

No Amber Alerts are being issued at this point, according to Insp. Jeff Allington at a news conference Saturday.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police directly at 416-808-4100.

World.title: Tens of thousands march in France as protests continue over schools and living costs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Protests in France continued a week after widespread rioting and looting across the country occurred during demonstrations over school funding and soaring living costs. In Paris, near the march's end point at Porte de Vincennes, some protesters threw projectiles while police fired volleys of tear gas and used water cannons to disperse people.

Tens of thousands march in France protests before police respond with tear gas and water cannons

Clashes erupted in Paris as a mass march drew to a close on Saturday, with more than 400,000 people rallying across France over school funding and soaring living costs in a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron's government.

The Paris march began peacefully, a week after widespread rioting and looting during protests across the country. Near its end point at Porte de Vincennes, some protesters threw projectiles while police fired volleys of tear gas and used water cannons to disperse people.

The Interior Ministry put nationwide turnout at 410,000, while the CGT union estimated nearly 800,000. The ministry's estimate included 110,000 in Paris, where authorities had confined the march to the city's southeastern edge, away from the centre.

Elsewhere in France, police used tear gas in several other cities, including Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand and Strasbourg, as well as water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Marseille, officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's end point.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police made nearly 1,000 arrests but added that the number is expected to increase significantly as more are counted.

Nuñez said beefed-up policing, with 70,000 officers backed by helicopters, armoured vehicles and other support, helped prevent a repeat of widespread looting and damage to shops that occurred during the previous weekend.

A police officer throws a tear gas canister during a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France, on Saturday. (Jeremias Gonzalez/The Associated Press)

The unrest is shaking Macron's authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May. The stakes are high: the far-right National Rally has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes.

In Paris, an Associated Press journalist saw tens of thousands of people marching from Porte d'Italie early in the afternoon, but it appeared to be a smaller crowd than a week earlier. Trade unions led the procession, followed by protesters in raincoats carrying flags and handmade placards.

More than half a million people took to the streets last Saturday. Around 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted over that weekend amid street violence not seen in years.

Museums closed, shopkeepers worried

Gendarmes stood guard beneath the Arc de Triomphe as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris on Saturday. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician's shop.

"I got the call last night," he said. "The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life."

Just Asking wants to know: What questions do you have about the wave of youth-led protests across Europe? Send us your questions before our Oct. 24 show

Major museums, including the Louvre, Musée d'Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — were shuttered Saturday.

Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.

WATCH | Here's why student in France started protesting this month: Why thousands of high school students in France are protesting | Duration 1:43 Police fired tear gas and water cannons at protesters blockading French high schools — as students, teachers, parents and unions took to the streets against what they say is underfunding of the education system. Rights groups and students have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government ‌has responded to the demonstrations with riot police and says the movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.

Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.

Some protests have been banned

Police changed the Paris protest route Friday. At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to tell people to leave or face a 135 euro (around $210 Cdn) fine.

Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, said she had been joining protests for more than 30 years but had never seen a march start at Porte d'Italie.

"They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters," she said. "But it won't stop the movement. It won't stop students from demanding better conditions in schools."

WATCH | Police used tear gas, water cannons during first round of protests: ‘It’s utter chaos': Protests in France evolve into anger over broader economy | Duration closed caption 2:21 Police in France used tear gas and arrested hundreds as widespread demonstrations over underfunding in schools evolved into scenes of anger and unrest over the cost of living.

A protest march was also scheduled in Marseille, but in cities including Nice and Montpellier, as well as Lyon, rallies were banned by the local authorities.

Thousands also marched Saturday in Orléans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as the National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.

Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.

Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.

Nuñez acknowledged Monday that police had lost control in some cities during last weekend's unrest. He offered to resign, but Macron refused the offer.

Students and workers are angry

Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system. Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.

They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros (around $310) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.

High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.

With the government seemingly unable to respond to students' demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron's successor.

"The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people," said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. "And it's not possible anymore."

Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.

Organizers from the "yellow vest" protest movement called for another day of rallies Oct. 31 to defend the right to demonstrate.

WATCH | France deployed riot police as students marched: Students in France clash with riot police amid weekslong education protests | Duration closed caption 3:26 Teachers formed a line to shield students from police in Paris, as countrywide protests over education reform have reached their fourth week.

Other protests rock major European cities

While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations are also rocking many European cities Saturday from Madrid to Milan, Lisbon and Tirana, Albania.

The protests encompass a broad range of issues from pensions and housing to anti-war movements, education and corruption.

People march through the streets of Milan on Saturday to protest against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services during one of several protests in Italy organized by groups across the political spectrum. (Antonio Calanni/The Associated Press)

In Milan, luxury boutiques were boarded up in the Italian fashion and finance capital as protesters launched fresh demonstrations on Saturday, one week after looting and clashes with police.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week.

Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.

A separate anti-war march took off in central Rome, and there are concerns over possible infiltration by violent groups.

Organizers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.

Aside from Rome and Milan, demonstrations have been called in at least seven other cities. The newly formed "Oct. 17 Movement" has been the main driver alongside student federations, grassroots trade unions, and anti-war coalitions.

In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 police officers are patrolling the streets Saturday.

World.title: Can millions of people live on the moon? These scientists say yes — but not for very long
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Humans have long dreamed about reaching out and exploring space. Most science fiction, more often than not, portrays cities on the dusty lunar surface and Mars.

And if you listen to some billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, cities on the moon are coming soon.

In fact, in February, SpaceX CEO Musk posted on social media that the company was shifting its focus away from settling on Mars — something Musk has been passionate about for the past decade.

“For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years,” he wrote.

For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the Moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years. The mission of SpaceX remains the same: extend consciousness and life as we know it to the stars. It is only possible to travel to Mars when the planets align every 26 months (six month trip time), whereas we can launch to the Moon every 10 days (2 day trip time). This means we can iterate much faster to complete a Moon city than a Mars city. That said, SpaceX will also strive to build a Mars city and begin doing so in about 5 to 7 years, but the overriding priority is securing the future of civilization and the Moon is faster. —elonmusk

This statement — and those of Blue Origin CEO Bezos, who has claimed “millions of people” will be living in space by 2045 — intrigued Martin Elvis, senior astrophysicist at Harvard University’s Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.

He, along with astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell, honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in England, decided to take a look at the numbers.

But their findings, it turns out, aren't great for a lunar civilization, so don’t start packing just yet.

In their paper , published in the journal Frontiers in Space Technologies, the pair decided to examine power and water needed to sustain humans on the moon.

When it comes to power, they found that solar and nuclear would be enough to sustain one million people on the lunar surface.

But then there's water.

It may be surprising to some, but there is water on the moon. It’s believed that most of it is contained in permanently shadowed regions (PSR), areas at the poles that never see sunlight.

But in this study, they found that there’s not enough on the moon to sustain a large human presence on the lunar surface.

WATCH | NASA shares plans for Moon Base: NASA shares plans for moon base | Duration closed caption 2:04 NASA has outlined its plans to build a base on the moon that will first be occupied by rovers and drones, but the longer-term goal is human habitation.

“Our work shows that, yeah, if you want to have an Antarctic base on the moon for the next few hundred years, no problem. If you want to have a small town, that's doable. If you want to cover the face of the moon with cities, like in the best science fiction, then you have to find a way to get the water there, because it's not there right now,” McDowell said.

Assuming that there is roughly one billion tonnes of water on the moon, which is in line with current estimates, they found that a civilization of one million people would only be able to live on the moon for roughly 100 years. And that’s only if we can recycle 98 per cent of the water, which is what is done on the International Space Station.

'A small lake'

Elvis said that while one billion tonnes of water sounds like a lot, you have to put it in perspective.

“If you had a huge aquarium the size of Central Park in Manhattan, you could fill it up to where the Statue of Liberty was just underwater and that's the amount of water you've got. So it's huge in one way, but … it's a small lake. And a small lake is not going to supply a big city for very long.”

That’s not to say that humans can’t ever live on the moon. If it were a town of 10,000, they found that would be sustainable for centuries.

However, that's assuming that the one billion tonnes of water is an accurate estimate.

"Very likely a billion is way overestimating. It's probably 20 or 30 times too big," Elvis said.

WATCH | How Artemis II is setting up the next stage of space exploration: How Artemis II is setting up the next stage of space exploration | Duration closed caption 4:42 Jacob Bleacher, NASA's chief exploration scientist, says the first two Artemis missions have set the stage for the next moon landing, a moon base and eventually, human exploration of Mars, missions so challenging that only international co-operation makes them possible.

He also said that it's unlikely that we'd be able to recover all the water that's available. Instead, it would be more like one-third to half of what is present.

"So my best guess is the real amount of water available that we can be fairly confident about is one per cent of what we said before. So instead of 100 years, it's one year."

And there's one other thing: We don't know in what form that water exists. And we need to figure that out.

"It's one thing to detect it from satellites, but ... there are uncertainties in those measurements," said Gordon Osinski, a professor in planetary geology at Western University in London, Ont.

" I think it is there, but let's go and ground-truth that and confirm it. And then there's the bigger unknowns of what form it's in…. Is it more like the permafrost up in the Arctic, where it's basically soil with, you know, sub-millimetre size ice crystals, which are hard to get out of?"

While this may sound like pessimistic news for humanity's plans to explore the cosmos, McDowell said it's best to know what you're dealing with.

"The truth is never negative," he said. "What's negative is to actually go and try and do something that isn't going to work."
