World.title: France: Clashes break out as protests go nationwide
World.content:
Skip next section French protests nowhere near the looting seen last weekend as yet, says DW reporter on the ground

Police and protesters are clashing in cities in France now too but the scale appears to be much smaller than the rioting seen last weekend (Photo: "We are the future of France") Image: Manon Cruz/REUTERS

The mood over the past few days in France felt almost a bit apocalyptic. Business owners told me they were worried more looting might lie ahead, after gangs of individuals had ransacked and destroyed at least 3,000 shops across the country last weekend.

"Some of us are planning to buy weapons to defend ourselves, in case the pillagers come back. One day, there's going to be a tragedy — for sure," Jonathan Siad, owner of a tobacco shop in Paris, said to me.

Other store owners were too afraid to talk to us in front of the camera – they worried criminals might see the interview and target their shop.

Residents told me they would try to avoid the area where the demonstration was taking place. Only to add that they hoped the situation wouldn't escalate like last week, when even places far away from the actual marches became hotspots of clashes between the police and protesters.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had admitted on Monday a "loss of control" last Saturday. The authorities thus increased the number of police deployed across France by 10,000 to 70,000 this Saturday.

First clashes between protesters and the police started to occur in the late afternoon in several cities across France such as Marseille, Lyon and Paris.

But for now, the much feared mass looting and ransacking doesn't seem to be happening. The situation is nowhere near the total chaos Paris and other cities like Marseille experienced last Saturday.

"Last weekend, our neighborhood resembled a war zone with gangs roaming the area. Today, it's completely empty apart from police with their vans," Yassaman Metghalchi, co-owner of a jewelry shop in the city center of Paris that got looted last Saturday, told me.

"All of our neighbors feel reassured – although the night is still young and we need to wait and see what will happen," she added.

World.title: Casi medio millón de personas mantiene el pulso a Macron en toda Francia pese al despliegue policial
World.content:
El ministro del Interior, pese a la tensión vivida en ciudades como París, Marsella o Lyon, se ha congratulado de una operación que ha dejado ya más de 1.000 detenidos y ha causado menos destrozos que hace una semana

Las protestas regresaron este sábado a Francia, donde confluyó de nuevo la rabia de estudiantes, parados, chalecos amarillos y funcionarios que lamentan el deterioro de la educación pública y el precio de la vida. Casi medio millón de personas, según el Ministerio del Interior (800.000, según el sindicato CGT) volvió a la calle para mantener el pulso al presidente Emmanuel Macron, que no ha dado ni una sola respuesta convincente a sus reivindicaciones. Lo hicieron desafiando un fuerte dispositivo policial, también a la lluvia y el mal tiempo. Y ocurrió todo pacíficamente, hasta que al final de algunas marchas, centenares de personas reeditaron escenas de confrontación y pillaje que devolvieron los ecos de la violenta protesta del sábado 17 de octubre, cuando más de 3.000 comercios fueron saqueados impunemente y edificios públicos, como el Ayuntamiento de Limoges, fueron destruidos por las llamas.

La noticia, más allá de la nota policial, señala que la protesta mantiene todo su vigor y promete seguir en la calle. No habrá tregua para el Ejecutivo. Los organizadores, apoyados por los chalecos amarillos, han vuelto a convocar marchas para el próximo 31 de octubre y 5 de noviembre. Esta última, acompañada de la propuesta de una huelga general. “Me preocupan esas fechas si no se toman medidas para satisfacer las reivindiaciones”, advirtió el alcalde de Marsella. Pero el problema es el mismo que hace un mes. No hay dinero en la caja. Francia arrastra una deuda del 119% del PIB y el Ejecutivo planea aprobar en los próximos días un presupuesto con 54.000 millones en recortes. Pero tampoco hay interlocutor fiable. A Macron, a quienes los manifestantes culpan de haber deteriorado los servicios públicos, le quedan seis meses en el cargo.

Los manifestantes prometían firmeza en París. Matthieu y Lux, alumnos de la Sorbona de 23 y 24 años (omiten su apellido), formaban parte de las miles de personas que se dirigían por la mañana a la Puerta de Vincennes en una gran marcha que evitó el centro de la ciudad. Pancarta contra el jefe del Estado —“Macron, rodarán cabezas”— y kufiya palestina al cuello, rechazaban la violencia de los últimos días, pero no se dan por vencidos en la calle. “Seguiremos volviendo el tiempo que haga falta. El Gobierno no escucha, solo responde con violencia. Cada sábado nos tendrán aquí”, anunciaban. Gilles y Laurence, 22 y 23 años, estudiantes de Ciencias Políticas, creen que “hay que apretar ahora. Si gana Marine Le Pen será todavía peor”.

A primera hora de la tarde, después de una mañana tranquila, comenzaron las cargas en varias ciudades como Grenoble, Niza, Estrasburgo, Lyon o Marsella. En París, donde unas 110.000 personas recorrieron la ciudad desde las 14.00 pacíficamente y bajo la lluvia, la policía empezó a disparar gases lacrimógenos y a dispersar a los manifestantes con cañones de agua.

El estruendo de las granadas aturdidoras, cuando parecía que no iba ocurrir, volvió a retumbar en la ciudad. Pero también en el discurso político de La Francia Insumisa (LFI), la única formación capaz de capitalizar políticamente esta protesta. “En París, para arruinar el día y relajarse, las llamadas fuerzas del orden lanzan gas lacrimógeno y disparan a ciegas al final del cortejo, con el objetivo de obtener imágenes para las cadenas nacionales que han difundido toda la semana las que motivaron al asesino de Trappes. La vergüenza en bucle”, lamentó su líder, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, presente en la manifestación, en referencia al asesinato racista ocurrido el pasado viernes en el extrarradio parisino.

Las protestas se intensificaron pasadas las cuatro de la tarde, también en otras urbes como Lyon o Marsella, donde la policía cargó y lanzó gases lacrimógenos. Hubo incendios, barricadas y proyectiles con morteros caseros por parte de los manifestantes. Mientras varios miles de personas seguían llegando a la plaza de la Porte-d’Aix, en la ciudad mediterránea, punto final de una manifestación que congregó a una multitud, se produjeron los enfrentamientos entre varias decenas de personas y los CRS (antidisturbios de la policía francesa). El alcalde de Marsella, Benoît Payan, restó importancia a los altercados y los calificó de “ligeros” en relación con la anterior semana, cuando y el Ayuntamiento fue vandalizado.

Francia estaba blindada. El Gobierno había desplegado 70.000 agentes en todo el país —prestando especial atención a París—, reforzados por el ejército, lo que no ocurría desde 2019, cuando se produjeron las protestas de los chalecos amarillos. Había drones, helicópteros y la reedición de un toque de queda a partir de las diez de la noche. A pesar de que la mañana había sido muy tranquila y los manifestantes habían marchado pacíficamente, hubo pillajes y saqueos en Marsella o Grenoble, barricadas e inmensas nubes blancas de gases lacrimógenos.

El ministro del Interior, Laurent Nuñez, visiblemente aliviado tras una semana muy señalado por los fallos de seguridad que dejaron más de 3.000 comercios saqueados, se congratuló por la efectividad del despliegue policial. “Gracias a la intervención de las fuerzas del orden, no se produjeron ataques contra edificios públicos, como ocurrió el 17 de octubre, ya fueran ayuntamientos (...), comisarías de policía”, se congratuló. A las 20.00, las fuerzas del orden habían detenido a más de 1.000 personas, el triple que una semana antes a la misma hora. El ministro, que cifró en 289 las manifestaciones en toda Francia, advirtió de que el número de detenidos iba a aumentar “de forma significativa”.

La lluvia y las medidas de seguridad, sin embargo, no disuadieron a los participantes más violentos de intentar saquear algún comercio y confrontar con la policía al término de la marcha. A media tarde, encapuchados y vestidos completamente de negro, se adueñaron de la protesta en París. Los enfrentamientos aumentaron y en Toulouse y en Clermont-Ferrand dos estudiantes fueron gravemente herido por la policía.

Un manifestante enmascarado, que sostiene un paraguas y una bandera francesa, reacciona mientras la policía francesa emplea un cañón de agua en medio de enfrentamientos durante una manifestación autorizada en París. Hannah McKay (REUTERS) La policía carga al finalizar la manifestación en Paris. Samuel Aranda Jóvenes durante los enfrentamientos con la policía al fin de la manifestación en Paris. Samuel Aranda Jóvenes en la manifestación de hoy en Paris. Samuel Aranda Manifestantes sostienen una bandera francesa y una bengala de humo durante una manifestación autorizada, organizada por un sindicato en Marsella. Manon Cruz (REUTERS) Personas se enfrentan a la policía durante una manifestación contra el alto costo de la vida en Burdeos. GUILLAUME PINON (EFE) La policía francesa carga contra varios manifestantes en Estrasburgo, este sábado. Jean-Francois Badias (AP Photo) Un policía sujeta a un manifestante durante la protesta a la altura de la Puerta de Italia en París. Mouneb Taim (Anadolu/Getty Images) Los manifestantes tras el despliegue de gases lacrimógenos, durante una manifestación no autorizada por las autoridades locales y convocada por el movimiento de los 'Chalecos Amarillos', a la que se sumaron estudiantes de secundaria y universidad franceses, en contra del coste de la vida y el aumento de los precios del combustible, en Lyon. Lisi Niesner (REUTERS) El candidato presidencial de la izquierda radical, Jean‑Luc Mélenchon, durante la manifestación celebrada en París. Abdul Saboor (REUTERS) Varias personas observan la manifestación desde una cafetería en la ciudad francesa de Orleans. Teresa Suarez (Associated Press/LaPresse) Varios manifestantes durante la jornada de protesta en Estrasburgo, este sábado. Jean-Francois Badias (Associated Press/LaPresse) Un manifestante sostiene una bandera frente a un cordón policial durante la manifestación organizada por los sindicatos franceses en París, este sábado. Hannah McKay (REUTERS) Varios manifestantes se suben a una marquesina durante la jornada de protestas de este sábado en París. Manu Brabo (Getty Images) Un manifestante tira una basura durante la manifestación de este sábado en Lyon. Lisi Niesner (REUTERS) Un manifestante sostiene una bandera francesa con el mensaje "Somos el futuro de Francia" en el Monumento de los Móviles, en Marsella, este sábado. Manon Cruz (REUTERS) Varios manifestantes participan en la protesta de este sábado, al margen del congreso del partido de extrema derecha Agrupación Nacional (RN), en Orleans (Francia). Teresa Suarez (Associated Press/LaPresse)

París, en cualquier caso, era el foco principal de preocupación del Ejecutivo. La capital, una de las pocas ciudades donde los sindicatos lograron que se autorizara la marcha, cerró 24 estaciones de metro desde las 9.00. Los comercios estaban cerrados a cal y canto y sus propietarios los habían vaciado. “Hemos metido la mercancía en una maleta y se la hemos dado a algunos vecinos”, explicaba Marine, propietaria de una tienda de bisutería a pocos metros de la plaza de la República.

Un manifestante sostiene una bandera frente a un cordón policial durante la manifestación organizada por los sindicatos franceses en París, este sábado. Hannah McKay (REUTERS)

La pelota vuelve ahora al tejado de la política. Macron se reunió el viernes por la tarde en el Palacio del Elíseo, durante dos horas y media, con una delegación de estudiantes. Fueron 150 minutos estériles, según sus representantes, que a la salida reiteraron que “la movilización constante” es “la única manera de lograr un progreso concreto”. “Nosotros hablamos de la derogación del Parcoursup [procedimiento de acceso a la educación superior], y él responde con una reforma total. Grandes promesas, palabras vacías”, señaló el responsable de la Unión Sindical de Estudiantes de Secundaria, Ryad Rani.

El ministro de Educación, Édouard Geffray, se reunirá de nuevo con los estudiantes el lunes para anunciar otras medidas. Pero la situación económica es crítica. El Banco de Francia modificó hace apenas unos días su previsión de crecimiento para 2026 hasta una horquilla de entre el 0,4% y el 0,5%, muy por debajo del 1% que manejaba a finales de 2025, y elevó su pronóstico de inflación hasta el 2,5% para este año, casi un punto porcentual más de lo calculado meses atrás. La propia entidad admite que esa atonía económica, combinada con el encarecimiento de la deuda, empujará el déficit público al 5,2% del PIB en 2026, una décima más que en 2025. La inflación interanual ya se situó en agosto en el 2,4%, acelerando desde el 2,1% de julio, con una energía que se ha encarecido casi un 17% en el último año.La agencia de calificación de deuda mantuvo la nota Aa3 a Francia el viernes por la noche con una perspectiva negativa hasta que se aclare la situación de tensión en la calle. Pero también en el Parlamento, donde las próximas semanas, en las que el Ejecutivo no tiene garantizada su continuidad, serán extremadamente convulsas.

La fragmentación política y la polarización crecen a pocos meses de los comicios presidenciales. Mientras las manifestaciones de los estudiantes tomaban de nuevo las calles, crecía la preocupación de que los disturbios pudieran alcanzar su máxima expresión en Orleans, la burguesa ciudad de las orillas del Loira donde el ultraderechista Reagrupamiento Nacional (RN) había convocado un congreso para lanzar la candidatura al Elíseo de su líder, Marine Le Pen, y confirmar a Jordan Bardella como presidente.

Varios trabajadores cubren con paneles la fachada de un comercio cerca de la plaza de la Bastilla, este sábado en París. Pedro Nunes (REUTERS)

La marcha, en la que participaron los líderes políticos de formaciones como el Parido Socialista (PS) se saldó sin incidentes. Pero mostró la enorme división política, que lleva incluso a partidos tradicional a manifestarse a las puertas del congreso de otra formación. “No entiendo nada. Nunca se me hubiera ocurrido ir a protestar contra otro partido, a asustar a sus militantes”, lamentó el vicepresidente del RN, Jean-Philippe Tanguy.

World.title: ¿Dónde y por qué se protesta en Europa? Las reivindicaciones de los jóvenes de cada país
World.content:
Estudiantes, sindicatos y vecinos han convocado más de 170 manifestaciones en poco más de un mes en todo el continente. Sus motivos a menudo coinciden

Media Europa vuelve a salir a la calle este sábado. Hay convocatorias desde Grecia hasta Bélgica, pasando por Albania, Francia, Portugal y España. Son las últimas de un otoño de movilizaciones: entre el 15 de septiembre y el 23 de octubre, 12 países europeos suman al menos 177 protestas o manifestaciones. La cifra es parecida a la media de 190 protestas mensuales entre septiembre y octubre de los otoños más intensos de la crisis del euro (2010, 2011 y 2012), según los registros de PolDem, un proyecto universitario que recopila protestas a partir de noticias de agencias. Francia, España, Italia, Portugal y Bélgica concentran la mayoría de las movilizaciones contabilizadas.

Las reivindicaciones cambian de un país a otro, pero tres se repiten de forma constante: la vivienda, la educación y el coste de la vida. Francia es ahora el centro de las concentraciones por la educación y el coste de la vida, y esas protestas se han extendido a Italia y Bélgica. En España, el foco es la vivienda: la primera gran manifestación del otoño se celebró el 26 de septiembre, tras el desahucio de Maricarmen, y reunió a al menos 25.000 personas en Madrid, según la Delegación del Gobierno (el Sindicato de Inquilinas contabilizó 300.000). Hasta esa fecha, fue la mayor protesta en una sola ciudad de este ciclo, y ha inspirado a manifestantes de Portugal e Italia. Al este del continente, los motivos son otros: la corrupción es el problema principal en Albania y en Serbia. En Alemania, las concentraciones son más pequeñas y se centran en la oposición al servicio militar y al rearme.

Images) Estudiantes se manifiestan contra la falta de recursos y personal en el sistema educativo, en la plaza de la República de París, el 4 de octubre de 2026. Veronique de Viguerie (Getty Images)

Los estudiantes han protagonizado buena parte de las protestas, pero se han ido sumando sindicatos, docentes y otros colectivos. Coinciden en el tiempo y comparten reivindicaciones, pero responden a conflictos nacionales distintos y no forman un movimiento coordinado. Que coincidan en otoño tiene una explicación en el calendario: “Los estudiantes vuelven a los centros, las redes organizativas se activan y los cambios en las tasas, las ayudas y las condiciones de estudio se vuelven inmediatamente tangibles”, explica Luka Lešić, de la Unión Europea de Estudiantes.

Los datos recopilados por EL PAÍS, a partir de agencias, medios y fuentes oficiales, incluyen las protestas contra medidas gubernamentales que reunieron al menos un centenar de personas y tuvieron cobertura en medios nacionales. Como se ve en el gráfico, los cinco países con más movilizaciones reúnen el 80% de las registradas.

La mayoría de las manifestaciones han sido pacíficas. Según los datos recopilados por este periódico, 49 protestas han terminado con detenidos y al menos 30 con agentes de la policía heridos. Ha habido episodios violentos en Italia, Albania y, sobre todo, Francia. Allí, la jornada del 17 de octubre reunió a 550.000 manifestantes en todo el país, según el Ministerio del Interior y terminó con más de 2.000 detenidos, casi 1.000 agentes heridos y destrozos importantes en varias ciudades, como el incendio del Ayuntamiento de Limoges. En Italia, el 18 de octubre, unos 2.000 jóvenes convocados por redes sociales, sin organización ni reivindicaciones políticas, irrumpieron en el centro de Milán para romper escaparates y saquear tiendas. La policía llevó a comisaría a 271, el 80% de ellos menores. Mientras, en Albania, más de 10 días de movilizaciones violentas han dejado el Tribunal Supremo, el Ministerio de Educación y otros edificios de la ciudad incendiados.

Manifestantes vandalizan un establecimiento durante unas protestas en Milán, Italia, el 18 de octubre de 2026. Andrea Carrubba (Anadolu/Getty Images)

A continuación, repasamos las causas y las razones de las reivindicaciones más transversales entre las protestas del continente.

Educación

En Francia, las protestas empezaron a mediados de septiembre con bloqueos de institutos y se extendieron en tres semanas a todo el país. El 1 de octubre hubo cientos de centros bloqueados. Los alumnos piden que se cubran las plazas de profesores vacantes —al comienzo del curso faltaba al menos uno en el 53% de los centros, según el sindicato docente SNES-FSU—, menos alumnos por clase y edificios en mejor estado. Este malestar social, en parte provocado por la necesidad de Francia de hacer recortes presupuestarios para reducir un elevado nivel de endeudamiento, ha cristalizado en el mayor movimiento de protesta en décadas.

La furia de los estudiantes franceses también encendió la ira de sus compañeros de la Bélgica francófona, que protestan desde octubre contra la subida de las tasas y los recortes presupuestarios, sobre todo en Bruselas y en Lieja. En prevención de posibles nuevos disturbios este fin de semana, Bruselas emitió una prohibición de circulación de patinetes y bicicletas eléctricas compartidas entre las diez de la mañana del viernes y las 22.00 del sábado en el centro de la ciudad.

En Italia salieron a la calle el 16 de octubre, entre otros motivos contra la norma que limita al 30% la presencia de determinadas categorías de alumnos extranjeros en las clases de primer curso. En Madrid, los profesores de la enseñanza pública están en huelga indefinida desde el 14 de octubre, y en Atenas más de 10.000 personas, según la policía, secundaron el día 21 una huelga de maestros.

Vivienda y coste de la vida

En España, a la acampada de Sol le siguió el 3 de octubre una jornada de marchas en medio centenar de ciudades, un día después de que el Congreso tumbara los dos decretos de vivienda del Gobierno. Los sindicatos mayoritarios convocaron una huelga general para el 11 de noviembre. En Portugal, las acampadas de Lisboa y Oporto pedían retirar un proyecto de ley que facilita los desahucios: la policía las ha desalojado el 20 de octubre.

El combustible movilizó a los transportistas del sur de Italia, que bloquean carreteras desde mediados de octubre, con el gasóleo a 2,30 euros el litro. En 2018, la subida de su impuesto ya llevó a la calle en Francia a los chalecos amarillos. En Alemania, los sindicatos reunieron el 26 de septiembre a 175.000 personas, según los convocantes, contra los recortes en pensiones y sanidad. La inflación se ha moderado desde el máximo de 2022, pero desde entonces los precios han subido un 23,6% en la UE, según Eurostat.

Corrupción

En Albania, la protesta empezó en mayo como un movimiento pacífico, la llamada revolución de los flamencos, contra la cesión de una reserva natural a empresarios vinculados con Jared Kushner, yerno de Donald Trump. Con el comienzo del curso, el 13 de octubre, se sumaron los estudiantes y las protestas se volvieron violentas: el 14 ardieron los ministerios de Educación y de Finanzas, y hasta el 19 hubo 310 heridos, según Europa Press. Piden la dimisión del primer ministro, Edi Rama, en el poder desde 2013, y acusan al Gobierno de proteger a grupos mafiosos. Ningún tribunal lo ha probado, aunque la Fiscalía investiga a la exviceprimera ministra, Belinda Balluku, por corrupción y blanqueo y el alcalde de Tirana, Erion Veliaj, permanece en prisión preventiva desde febrero de 2025, acusado de los mismos cargos.

Manifestantes hablan con agentes de policía durante una protesta antigubernamental de estudiantes en Tirana, Albania, el 20 de octubre de 2026. Louisa Gouliamaki (REUTERS)

En Serbia, el movimiento estudiantil ha madurado a lo lago de dos años en las calles, después de la muerte de 16 personas en el derrumbe de la estación de Novi Sad, en noviembre de 2024. Sus demostraciones forzaron al Gobierno de Aleksandar Vucic a adelantar las elecciones, convocadas para este domingo. El movimiento se presenta como Lista de Estudiantes y es la segunda fuerza, según la última encuesta de Ipsos. El jueves, unas 150.000 personas se concentraron en Belgrado, según recuentos independientes.

La respuesta de los gobiernos

En Francia, el Gobierno decretó toques de queda en París y otras ciudades, y también anunció más de 3.000 profesores suplentes y retiró la subida de algunas tasas universitarias. Para este sábado, el Ejecutivo solo ha autorizado las marchas sindicales y ha prohibido las concentraciones en Lyon y Marsella, con un despliegue policial un 20% mayor que el del 17 de octubre.

En Italia, el decreto de seguridad ya castigaba la participación violenta en una manifestación con hasta cinco años de prisión, y de cara a la jornada de hoy las autoridades han blindado el centro de Milán y las estaciones de la periferia desde las que llegaron los jóvenes.

La policía lleva a cabo detenciones y arrestos de los manifestantes tras las protestas contra el alto costo de la vida en Milán, Italia, el 18 de octubre de 2026. Andrea Carrubba (Anadolu/ Getty Images)

Las próximas citas llegan en noviembre: una jornada sindical en Francia el día 5, una jornada estudiantil en Alemania el 17, la huelga general del sindicato CGIL en Italia el 20 y, en Portugal, una manifestación de la CGTP ante el Parlamento portugués el 24. Además de la huelga general convocada en España para el 11 de noviembre.

Con información de Raquel Villaécija, desde París; Silvia Ayuso, desde Bruselas; Francisco Peregil, desde Tirana, e Íñigo Domínguez, desde Roma.

World.title: Países Bajos no está hecho para los tanques
World.content:
Países Bajos, la quinta economía de la UE, suele presentarse como la puerta de entrada al continente debido a su ubicación junto a Francia, Bélgica y Alemania, y el mar del Norte. También, por la pujanza del puerto de Róterdam y el aeropuerto de

Ámsterdam-Schiphol, y por el servicio de trenes que conecta con Bruselas, Londres o Fráncfort en pocas horas. En caso de que hubiera una guerra en suelo europeo, sin embargo, ese emplazamiento privilegiado pasaría a convertirse en estratégico, y las rutas de tránsito militar (corredores, en lenguaje técnico) no cumplen con los acuerdos de la OTAN para grandes transportes. Se trata de una red de carreteras, puentes y ferrocarriles que necesitan una inversión de al menos 9.500 millones de euros para mejoras, según el Tribunal de Cuentas, que ha publicado este mes un informe a la vista del aumento de la inestabilidad geopolítica en Europa.

Sin un hipotético panorama bélico sobre la mesa, el Gobierno neerlandés afronta ya un déficit total de 80.000 millones de euros para proyectos de equipamientos a escala nacional, tal y como indica la carta remitida en marzo pasado al Congreso por el ministerio de Infraestructuras y Gestión del Agua. “No se puede hacer todo, ni se puede hacer todo al mismo tiempo”, dijo entonces su titular, Vincent Karremans, que hizo un llamamiento al Parlamento para “tomar juntos decisiones difíciles”.

De producirse un conflicto, gran parte de los recursos militares de la OTAN entrarían en Europa a través de los puertos neerlandeses, pero las carreteras, vías férreas y puentes que deberían usarse para ello no pueden resistir ese tipo de tráfico. Se trataría de tanques, vehículos más pequeños o sistemas de armamento, y entre los requisitos militares señalados por el alto mando de la OTAN “se incluyen, por ejemplo, las alturas de los viaductos o los puentes ferroviarios que soporten vagones con cargas pesadas”, según reza el informe del Tribunal de Cuentas. El cálculo de sus expertos cifra la inversión necesaria “en 4.500 millones de euros en mejoras de las que también se beneficiarían los ciudadanos”. Unos 5.000 millones de euros adicionales se destinarían a “cumplir con los requisitos militares”.

En 2023, la UE designó una serie de corredores en Europa destinados al transporte rápido de material militar. El Tribunal de Cuentas advierte de que algunos vehículos de grandes dimensiones no podrían circular por la parte neerlandesa de esas rutas especiales. Bien porque las carreteras son hoy demasiado estrechas, o porque los puentes no aguantarían el peso. En el caso del ferrocarril, el informe señala que como esta clase de material precisa de un transporte más ancho, “los trenes que circulen en sentido contrario no podrían hacerlo, o tendrían que desviarse”, con el consiguiente disturbio y retrasos para la ciudadanía.

Sin recursos para invertir

En tiempo de paz también hay transportes militares regulares, y el Servicio Nacional de Trafico colabora con el Ministerio de Defensa para adaptarse al estado diario del tráfico. En caso de conflicto, tener que cambiar de ruta puede suponer un problema si una pasarela es demasiado baja, un puente necesita reparaciones o unas traviesas están hundidas en algún tramo de la vía del tren. En su respuesta por carta al Tribunal de Cuentas, el ministro Karremans abunda en el hecho de que “gran parte de la infraestructura nacional está obsoleta y con necesidad de mantenimiento”, pero “no se dispone de recursos financieros suficientes para ponerla a punto al ritmo necesario”. De ahí que se esté llevando a cabo una “reordenación de las prioridades”, para el mantenimiento de las infraestructuras “que garanticen el transporte militar a gran escala a través del país”, y para mantener a su vez “el funcionamiento de la sociedad con la mayor normalidad posible”. Si bien el trazado exacto de los corredores militares es secreto por razones de seguridad, Defensa colgó en 2021 en su web una nota donde decía que “se habilitarán tres distribuidos geográficamente por Países Bajos”, que incluyen vías por carretera, ferrocarril y vías navegables, adaptadas al material más grande y pesado.

World.title: More sleep on Sunday as clocks go back an hour
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Everyone is due an extra hour’s sleep on Sunday as the clocks will roll back an hour at 3am to 2am.

Daylight saving time in the Netherlands has been in place since 1977, following the oil crisis of the 70s, when saving energy on lighting became a priority.

The clocks go forward in spring, on the last Sunday of March, to give lighter evenings. Staying on summer time into the winter would mean very dark mornings, so in October the clocks return to standard time.

The EU has debated ending daylight saving time altogether and the European Parliament voted to stop it in 1996 but member states have not yet committed to it.

So tomorrow you can lie in a little longer.

World.title: Egypt protests shut Dutch embassy over arrest of Sisi loyalist
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch embassy in Cairo has closed to the public until further notice after nine days of protests outside the building, during which staff had to be evacuated, the embassy has announced on social media.

The demonstrators are demanding the release of Ahmed Nasser, deputy head of a pro-government Egyptian youth group, who was arrested in the Netherlands on October 10.

He was reportedly detained on suspicion of threatening Anas Habib, an Egyptian activist who lives in the Netherlands, and his pre-trial detention has been extended by 14 days, broadcaster NOS reported.

Habib drew international attention last summer when he filmed himself padlocking the gates of the Egyptian embassy in The Hague, in protest at the Egyptian government keeping the Rafah border crossing with Gaza closed.

His action sparked similar protests at Egyptian embassies in more than 16 countries, after which supporters of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi began gathering outside embassies to “protect” them.

Days after Nasser’s arrest, Egyptian foreign minister Badr Abdelatty called his Dutch counterpart to demand his release and better protection for Egypt’s embassy in The Hague.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said on social media that the two had “discussed the need for progress on the security of our respective embassies and consular affairs.”

It is unclear exactly how Nasser is alleged to have threatened Habib.

World.title: Getting home safely: ADE festivals step up protection measures
World.content:
With the Amsterdam Dance Event (ADE), the world’s biggest electronic music event, underway, extra safety measures have been put in place by festival organisers and the city to make sure, Amsterdam says, that everyone feels “safe in the nightlife scene – free from any form of harassment, violence, discrimination, or (sexual) misconduct.”

To that end, there is a host of initiatives at various festival sites where techno lovers can recharge or get help getting home safely.

Bike buddies, hosts and Check-Ins

At the DGTL festival on NDSM island, cycling buddies will be on hand to help people get safely back and forth to the ferries. They will be working in pairs to ensure their own safety.

A Safe Check-In on NDSM wharf will be open all night for people who need physical help, feel unsafe at night or just need a breather. Phones can also be charged there.

At Awakenings in Halfweg, a Goodbye Host will be stationed at the exit, keeping a watchful eye on partygoers leaving solo. Hosts can help with route planning, and phones can also be charged here.

Both locations will also feature an Awareness Crew, trained teams identifiable by badges or vests that offer support to those feeling uncomfortable or unsafe.

Taking back the night

Some of the safety measures are not new. Last year, following the August murder of teenager Lisa while she cycled home alone and the resulting Take Back the Night campaign, the biking buddies programme was set up.

“We’ve been running social safety measures at our events since Covid, through our awareness teams and social safety hub, so this is something we’ve prioritized for a long time already,” Nikki Schuurs, who deals with Social Safety at DGTL, told Dutch News.

“Bike Buddies, however, was indeed introduced in response to the Take Back the Night campaign, following the murder of Lisa. Safety doesn’t stop at the dance floor.”

Visitors can find the Bike Buddy meeting point just outside the event. Group rides depart every 30 minutes between 21:00 and 07:00, on the hour and half-hour.

Safety concerns have again risen in the city following the violent death of 29-year-old Hajar, whose body was found in a suitcase in the Amstel River last week. She had last been seen cycling with a man near the RAI convention centre. He has since been arrested in connection with her death.

World.title: Inburgering with Dutch News: the great cycle path squeeze
World.content:
You can’t have failed to notice that Dutch cycle paths are no longer the preserve of old-fashioned cyclists. E-bikes, fatbikes, scooters, snorfietsen, speed pedelecs, disabled vehicles – a seemingly never-ending stream of other road users have moved in. But what exactly are the rules and regulations?

Lesson 64: what is allowed on the cycle path?

Fatbike

The fatbike, with its characteristic thick tyres and frequently thick riders, has become wildly popular. It’s not surprising because at the moment, riders do not need a helmet, driving licence, or third-party liability insurance. The fatbike is officially an e-bike, and therefore there is no age limit, but measures are afoot to make helmet-wearing compulsory for riders up to the age of 18.

Fatbikes are allowed to travel at up to 25 kph. However, many are doctored to go faster – as you will notice when you see them whizzing past cars that keep to the 30 kph limit, mandatory for cars in some Dutch cities.

Electric bike

The electric non-fat bike, so to speak, is literally overtaking the person-powered bike, and that is partly due to its popularity among older riders – who are also well represented in the annual traffic death toll. The same rules of the road as apply to fatbikes apply to ordinary e-bikes – none. You will, however, see more and more elderly riders with a helmet.

Electric cargo bike

The cargo bike, or moedermobiel, deserves a separate mention because of the riders’ mistaken opinion that everyone has to make way for this space-hogging vehicle because it carries cute little toddlers. A good place to spot cargo bikes is outside primary schools at 3pm, when they cause a veritable jam of their own.

Speed pedelec

Speed pedelecs are electric bikes as well, but unlike normal electric bikes, they can legally reach speeds of up to 45 kph. This makes them motorcycles in the eyes of the law, with the rules that then apply, such as mandatory helmet-wearing, a driving licence and insurance. Speed pedelecs can travel on cycle paths, but only at a maximum of 25 kph.

Snorfiets, or moped

No pedalling is needed for this motorised bike or moped, which has a maximum speed limit of 25 kph and is allowed on cycle paths. Although snorfietsen have the same speed limit as electric bikes, they are technically considered to be motorcycles, and riders need a helmet, a driving licence and insurance.

The introduction of helmets for all types of mopeds several years ago led to the downfall of the snorfiets – after all, if you need a helmet, why not drive a proper motorbike – or a fatbike?

Scootmobiel

The motorised wheelchair or scootmobiel is possibly the most dangerous vehicle on the cycle path. According to statistics agency CBS, the traffic death rate among mobility scooter riders is over six times that of motorbike riders and over 20 times that of cyclists.

Users don’t need to pass any tests or learn the rules of the road, and they can go pretty much wherever they like – shopping centre, pavement, cycle path, ordinary road – just not the motorway.

The Canta

The Canta looks like a brommobiel – a small electric vehicle with four wheels – but because it is considered a mobility aid for people with a disability, it is treated in the same way as a scootmobiel.

The Canta is not supposed to go faster than 30 kph on the cycle path and 45 kph on the road, but is allowed to mount the pavement and annoy pedestrians at 6 kph. It can also park anywhere and does not need a number plate.

The minimum age is 16, and you’ll need to take out insurance, but you don’t need a driving licence. The Canta became popular with youngsters who could not be bothered to cycle and has since spawned a surge in far hipper micro cars.

Micro cars

The Birò and its ilk are small, fashionable and, according to many, extremely annoying electric vehicles which are banned from cycle paths but whose drivers use them anyway – particularly as a sneaky escape when faced with a traffic jam.

Popular with estate agents and PR people, micro cars have a maximum speed of 45 kph. If you want one, you will need a brommobiel driving licence and must be 16 or over.

Electric scooter

The step, or scooter, used to be a children’s plaything, but since the invention of the electric version, they have been taking over cities throughout Europe. Steps which have been officially approved have been allowed on Dutch cycle paths since July 1 this year. In Dutch terminology they are known as “light electric vehicles”.

The step has a maximum speed of 25 kph, and riders have to be 16 or over. You will need third-party liability insurance, and the base must have a number plate which is clearly visible.

The e-step is predicted to rival the fatbike in popularity and ability to provoke cycle-path rage – as long as helmets are not compulsory.

World.title: Amsterdam exploring single-use packaging ban
World.content:
Amsterdam is considering banning single-use packaging, including coffee cups, fast-food containers and other single-use plastics that it says make up 30% of the city’s litter.

“Litter is a persistent problem; it is a symptom of a ‘throwaway society’ that pollutes our beautiful city and costs millions every year,” said Amsterdam executive Lian Heinhuis, who is responsible for waste and sanitation, in a statement.

“Yet the solution is within reach: putting an end to the throwaway culture.”

To that end, the city has commissioned a study into what it can legally do to tackle the problem. According to CircuLaw, which provides legal information on circular transitions, such a ban could be implemented, but only after less restrictive measures have proven not to work.

A ban also works best alongside other measures, such as a reliable supply of reusable packaging and a well-established return system.

The city says it will work with business owners and residents and also look at how other cities are managing the problem, including Copenhagen and Lisbon, the latter of which has already implemented a single-use packaging ban.

“Single-use packaging is a major problem,” the city said. “The plastics used in these items take hundreds of years to decompose – if they ever do at all. They pollute the soil and groundwater for a very long time, despite being used for an average of only about seven minutes.”

World.title: Student union furious as minister says interest cap unaffordable
World.content:
Despite a coalition promise to cap student loan interest rates at 2.5%, education minister Rianne Letschert has told parliament that the government can no longer afford to stick to its pledge.

The minister said that capping the interest rate at 2.5% is risky and expensive, and that the €40 million annual budget the coalition had set aside to cover the cap is only a quarter of what it would actually cost – €160 million – and could lead to other cuts in the education budget.

“I understand the concerns of current and former students regarding the rise in interest rates on student debt, driven by global instability and an increase in long-term interest rates,” Letschert said in a statement on Thursday.

“Unfortunately, I must conclude that it is not possible to implement a 2.5% interest rate cap with the €40 million per year that has been set aside. I find this very disappointing.”

Geopolitical costs

Since the coalition agreement was first presented at the end of January, the global landscape has significantly shifted due to geopolitical tensions and financial uncertainty. Long-term interest rates – to which student loan rates are linked – have risen from 2.7% to 3.3% and could climb higher.

“Recent shocks in the financial markets highlight just how unpredictable – and potentially financially risky – this interest rate policy is,” the ministry said.

But students aren’t buying it. “This effectively sends students out into the world burdened by an incredibly heavy backpack of debt,” LSVB, the national student union, told news service ANP. “The only certainty this cabinet offers students is the assurance that interest rates will rise even further in the coming years.”

Student union ISO added that once again, “students are the victims of empty promises.”

Letschert will discuss the issue with parliament later this month.

World.title: Cyber security centre warns PHP hacking situation could worsen
World.content:
The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is investigating the first signs of successful hacks on websites following the exposure of critical vulnerabilities on the web, and says the situation could “rapidly worsen”.

A spokesperson told the Volkskrant on Thursday that the signals came from the NCSC’s international network, and that there was no sign yet of abuse involving Dutch websites. The centre is still checking whether the reports are accurate.

Cybersecurity researchers, working with the help of AI, found that PHP, the programming language on which a majority of the web is built, had at least two serious vulnerabilities in its code.

Details of the weaknesses were leaked online on Monday, and the PHP developers announced they would issue an upgrade by Wednesday afternoon.

Hacking attempts began even before the leak, with Amazon reporting an attack attempt on October 17. US internet security firm Cloudflare said it saw hacking attempts run from thousands before the upgrade to millions afterwards.

Initially, the NCSC said that there were no signs of active hacks and the PHP developers said there were no indications of breaches.

Large amounts of government, healthcare and news sites were forced to go dark temporarily while awaiting the upgrade, including Dutch News.

The Netherlands was fast to act, closing a large amount of its sites and issuing warnings early on Wednesday, after which governments in Belgium, Germany, France and Finland did the same. The issue is now a global concern.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP said on Thursday it had not yet received any reports of data breaches linked to the vulnerabilities.

World.title: Leader of junior coalition partner quits Polish government
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced that her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday. Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term. Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku! Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi… — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026 Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday. Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power. However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them. Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all. Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party. “The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.” “I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.” Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down. However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen. In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre). Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk. Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus. They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026 On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”. The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”. Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority. W @PL_2050 dowiedzieliśmy się o decyzji @Kpelczynska z mediów. Zaskakująca rezygnacja przewodniczącej z zaufania wyborców i odpowiedzialności powierzonej jej w bardzo trudnym momencie przez ludzi (w tym mnie) zaledwie po niespełna 1/3 kadencji – dla każdej organizacji byłaby… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 22, 2026 The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues. It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%. In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 The fact that the bill to end two-term limits for mayors was defeated has also caused tension between PSL and its coalition partners. In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives. The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk. World.title: Protesters return to Poland’s streets demanding liberalisation of abortion law
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws. However, the demonstrations, which took place on the sixth anniversary of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) ruling that introduced a near-total abortion ban, were nowhere near the scale of the massive protests that emerged back in 2020. Było deszczowo, ale nie brakowało ludzi i emocji. Rzeszów pokazał czerwoną kartkę za aborcję rządzącej koalicji. pic.twitter.com/oJo8BiWXxS — Paweł Preneta (@pawelpreneta) October 22, 2026 In Warsaw, a few hundred people gathered in the rain outside parliament, reported broadcaster RMF. Many held up red cards, a symbol used by the protesters to warn the government that it could be thrown out of power at next year’s parliamentary elections. When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition. Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear. Parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland's abortion laws One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling that introduced a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise helping women in obtaining unlawful abortions https://t.co/nVj8SQVIsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, around 1,000 people attended Thursday’s protest, according to police estimates cited by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Among the placards and banners was one showing Tusk with an extended, Pinocchio-style nose. “It’s sad that we have to engage in this fight again,” said one of the organisers. “For so long, they ignored us, only coming when they needed votes. Now let’s show that we can’t be ignored.” In Katowice, around 300 people gathered, according to the Polish Press Agency (PAP). In Poznań, around 400 or so protesters marched to the local headquarters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, where they placed a symbolic red card and waved banners saying “You deceived Poland”. Czerwona kartka za aborcje. W #Lodz w proteście w strugach deszczu protestuje kilkadziesiąt osób @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/okU7QjnhFw — Mateusz Szkudlarek (@m_szkudlarek) October 22, 2026 The 2020 TK abortion ruling triggered the largest protests seen in Poland since the communist era, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets. That anger is seen as having played a major role in PiS losing power to Tusk’s coalition in 2023. Opinion polls consistently show that most Poles want the abortion law to be liberalised, though there remain divisions over whether there should be a return to the pre-2021 status quo or a move even further, to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In autumn 2027, parliamentary elections will take place, deciding who governs Poland for the next four years. Opinion polls currently show a fairly even split in support between Tusk’s coalition and the right-wing opposition. World.title: Poland charges second Georgian man over murder of Russian dissident
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year. The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself. Warto przypomnieć: ▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości. ▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026 Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin. He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons. After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused. On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then. Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week. "Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway. The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban. Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN. The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”. Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty. A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”. However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026 The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”. In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations. Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia. Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states. World.title: Poland and India aim to double trade by 2030 as PMs meet in New Delhi
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies. Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades. During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”. Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies. Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20. “The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said. Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.” Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market. Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”. “Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.” However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals. The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible". "Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility. To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations. Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people. The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations. Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War. “In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”. The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year.
