The last time Sydney netball fans had the chance to support a home team in a league grand final was 18 years ago in the former ANZ Championship. The Super Netball league was nearly a decade away from foundation when a six-year-old Amy Sligar, who now plays for the Sydney Sirens, watched the NSW Swifts defeat the Waikato Bay of Plenty Magic 65-56 in July 2008. Sydney will host the Super League netball grand final next year, much to the delight of Amy Sligar from the Sydney Sirens, Grace Whyte from the Swifts and Netball Australia boss Mark Falvo. James Brickwood “I would have watched that game with stars in my eyes and probably my heroes were playing in that game,” she said. Though the Swifts would appear in two more grand finals of the ANZ Championship and go on to play in three of the Super Netball grand finals since the league began in 2017 none were in Sydney. Neither were the two other grand finals a Sydney team featured in.



But Sligar, now 24, has the chance to play a final at home in 2027. On Sunday, Netball Australia and the NSW government will announce that the 2027 grand final will be held on July 31 at Afterpay Arena at Sydney Olympic Park, the same venue will then host the Netball World Cup a month later. The Adelaide Thunderbirds celebrate their 2026 Super Netball title win in Melbourne. Getty Images “Netball is one of the biggest participation sports in NSW, with thousands of kids and adults taking to the court every week, and it deserves the same attention and support we give our other major sport,” NSW Premier Chris Minns said on Sunday. “For too long, we haven’t invested enough in netball and we’re working to change that – from grassroots facilities and participation right through to bringing the biggest events in the sport to NSW.”



The state government expects the grand final will bring 8000 spectators to Sydney to watch at the 18,000-capacity arena, adding what they estimate to be more than $4 million to the economy. The World Cup in August will see a target of 200,000 attendees to watch Australia’s Diamonds defend their 2023 title. The state government has also set up a $1.5 million World Cup legacy program for players, coaches and officials. Minister for Sport Steve Kamper said the events would make the city the centre of the netball world next year. Netball Australia chief executive Mark Falvo said 2027 will be huge for netball fans in Sydney. Sligar said knowing the grand final will be held at home provides extra motivation for the season ahead, especially over local rivals the Swifts.



“My first reaction is that it makes me want to make the grand final even more to have a home grand final,” she said. “You almost couldn’t write a better script to have a new Sydney team [the Sirens] and then Sydney hosting the grand final, Sydney hosting the World Cup this year.” “I think for young boys and girls and men and women to be able to come and see the world’s best netball, it just builds excitement on the sport.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘National suicide’: The election issue tearing Israelis apart
World.content:
A row over whether a Jerusalem coffee shop could open on the Sabbath escalated into an epic culture war. For modern Israel, it could be the shape of things to come.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Jerusalem/ Bnei Brak: Almost anywhere else in the world, a cafe opening for business on Saturday would not be an inflammatory act. But in downtown Jerusalem, Cafe Basimta’s decision to sell coffee and pastries on the Sabbath ignited an almighty culture war between the Holy City’s ultra-Orthodox and secular residents. Soon after the coffee shop opened in a quiet alley in May, dozens of ultra-Orthodox teenage boys wearing black suits and fedoras showed up to block its entrance while chanting “Whoever breaks the Sabbath has no part in the world to come”. A young ultra-Orthodox protester stands his ground outside Cafe Basimta while counter-protesters make their point. The cafe has now decided to stay shut on Saturdays. AFP Ultra-Orthodox Jews believe in resting on the Sabbath, the frequent study of religious texts, strict gender segregation and eating kosher, pitting them against the less devout, who favour a more relaxed approach. As the demonstrations grew each week, so did counter-protests. Hundreds of non-religious activists locked arms to protect the entrance to the café, and prominent politicians from the right and left joined in. The fact that the cafe’s owners – the messianic and controversial Jews for Jesus organisation – were hardly secular was a wrinkle in the narrative. But it didn’t deter most of the counter-protesters, who believed they were fighting for an important principle. The argument raging over whether coffee and pastries could be sold on the Jewish sabbath became a microcosm of a wider debate about competing rights in modern Israel. AFP



“We see it as our right to be able to drink coffee on the Sabbath in the centre of Jerusalem,” says deputy Jerusalem mayor Adir Schwarz, a champion of the city’s secular population. “Our capital is supposed to unite all Israelis, and if any Jew is being pushed out of Jerusalem, that is a bad forewarning for the rest of the state of Israel.” While the havoc was a boon for business, the owners ultimately decided it wasn’t worth the pain. In September, the cafe announced it would no longer open on Saturdays. “The cafe has become, over the past several months, a focal point of friction and danger,” Jews for Jesus chief executive Eli Birnbaum said. Strict ultra-Orthodox modesty laws have brought the community into conflict with the 21st century. Disappointed by the decision, secular activists mostly abandoned the cafe and business plummeted. When we visited last week, the coffee was excellent, but only a handful of customers were there. Schwarz says the backdown was just the latest blow to secular Jerusalemites, who feel increasingly marginalised and disempowered. Ultra-Orthodox residents are rising in number and moving into secular suburbs, sparking heated battles over resources and cultural norms. ‘We live in separate worlds, and those worlds are getting further apart’ Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser “A territorial battle is playing out in certain neighbourhoods as their identity changes and becomes more religious,” Schwarz says.



Schwarz cites strict ultra-Orthodox modesty laws which can expose female pedestrians to harassment and intimidation for wearing jeans. “The fact a secular woman cannot walk in pants through the neighbourhood she grew up in is a big problem,” Schwarz argues. Children in Bnei Brak. The birthrate for ultra-Orthodox Jews now vastly exceeds that of other groups. Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community – known as the Haredim – makes up 14 per cent of the national population. That figure is exploding, reflecting the fact that the birth rate for ultra-Orthodox women (6.5 children per woman) is vastly higher than for other Jewish women (2.2 children). By 2065, the Haredim are projected to comprise a third of Israeli society, a figure unimaginable when Israel was founded in 1948. Such rapid growth equals more political power but also greater scrutiny about ultra-Orthodox Jews’ contribution to Israeli society. Twenty minutes from central Tel Aviv, Bnei Brak is a world away from modern Israel. The fight over Cafe Basimta is emblematic of a deeper battle being waged in Israel ahead of national elections on Tuesday. Topics that foreigners may expect to be front-of-centre – like how Israel waged its war on Gaza or the possibility of a two-state solution with the Palestinians – are almost entirely absent from the public discourse. Meanwhile, the concessions provided to ultra-Orthodox Israelis are tearing the nation apart and dominating the campaign. Bnei Brak is a mere 20-minute drive from the gay bars and non-kosher restaurants of Tel Aviv, but it might as well be on a different planet. “We live in separate worlds, and those worlds are getting further apart,” Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser says of the two cities, which serve as avatars for Israel’s ultra-Orthodox and secular tribes. Here there is none of the clashing and intermingling you find in more integrated Jerusalem. Bnei Brak Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser says he is alarmed by the push for compulsory military service for the ultra-Orthodox community, who are currently exempt. Vered Adir



Bnei Brak is one of the world’s most densely populated cities: 230,000 people, almost all of them Haredi, crammed into just seven square kilometres of land. “It’s a terrible city, it’s dirty, it’s more crowded than Gaza,” Goldwasser says as he slurps a bowl of matzo ball soup. His kosher phone, which blocks internet access, sits on the table. On the plus side, he says it is a self-contained society packed with restaurants, yeshivas, shops and medical facilities where the streets remain lively until the early hours of the morning. In Hebrew, the Haredim means those who tremble before God. To be ultra-Orthodox is to be on edge. But Goldwasser says the community’s naturally high anxiety has spiked to intolerable levels because of an all-out campaign to force them to serve in the military. The dilemma of ultra-Orthodox army service has existed before the founding of Israel in 1948. To ensure as broad support as possible for the creation of a Jewish state, founding prime minister David Ben-Gurion granted 400 yeshiva students exemptions from compulsory military service. This reflected the ultra-Orthodox community’s fraught relationship with Zionism (many believe establishing a sovereign Jewish state before the arrival of the Messiah violates divine law). Related Article Exclusive

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Like a wounded animal’: Netanyahu will do whatever it takes to stay in power, former PM warns A decade later, with thousands of students now exempt, Ben-Gurion questioned his decision. Today, court filings by Israel’s attorney-general estimate that about 80,000 are avoiding military service. This became a source of fury as Israel fought a multi-front war against its enemies after the October 7 attacks of 2023. The burdens of service – time spent away from family and the risk of dying on the battlefield – have not been distributed evenly across society. Reflecting the new era Israel entered after October 7, the Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that the longstanding blanket exemption for yeshiva students was unlawful. Fierce resistance has followed. Last year, chief rabbi Yitzhak Yosef used his weekly sermon to warn that the ultra-Orthodox community “will all board planes and leave Israel” if they are forced to serve in the army.



Attempts to force Haredi men to enlist, including through arrests, have sparked riots and blockades of major highways. In June, ultra-Orthodox rioters smashed windows, damaged flowerpots, and vandalised a car parked at the home of the Supreme Court’s deputy president. Elchanan Wasserman says his story proves you can be ultra-Orthodox and serve in the Israeli military. “As far as they’re concerned, it’s life or death. Religion comes first,” Wasserman says, explaining why the issue arouses such passion. Bnei Brak yeshiva student Yakov, 20, says he has no intention of enlisting. “Prison, sanctions, nothing can break us,” he declares. His dream is to be a rabbi. Protests and arrests have accelerated in the lead-up to the October 27 election, raising the temperature. The military arrested 40 ultra-Orthodox men returning from the United States on Tuesday at Tel Aviv airport on suspicion of draft dodging. An ultra-Orthodox Jew burns an Israeli flag as anti-government amid protests against their military service exemptions. Getty Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose conservative coalition is reliant on ultra-Orthodox parties, criticised the arrests. “We need to preserve the world of Torah study because it has preserved us,” he said in a radio interview. On the other side of the debate, the four main Jewish parties running against Netanyahu are all campaigning to end sweeping exemptions from military service. They are convinced they are onto a vote winner. An overwhelming 72 per cent of Israelis want to see the Haredim drafted alongside other Israelis eligible for military service, according to a September poll by the Israel Democracy Institute.

World.title: Meghan ‘upset’ by police failure to act on letter about father
World.content:
WorldEuropeMeghan, Duchess of Sussex Meghan ‘upset’ by police failure to act on letter about father Hannah Furness , Patrick Sawer and Victoria Ward October 25, 2026 — 9:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: The Duchess of Sussex is “upset and frustrated” after the Metropolitan Police admitted it had failed to act on sex abuse allegations against her father, the London Telegraph has revealed. The duchess, whose father, Thomas Markle, has been accused of serious offences against children in the Philippines, has been aware of separate allegations since January 2019, but police are said to have told her not to discuss them publicly. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, says she was informed years ago about “disturbing allegations” about her father, Thomas Markle. Getty; Supplied Scotland Yard confirmed on Saturday that it received a letter “containing a number of claims about alleged offending” outside its British jurisdiction, but admitted it had not passed it on to overseas authorities. The force is now considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct over how the letter was handled.



According to the Telegraph, when Meghan wrote to her father while he was in hospital last year, she accused him of being unsafe around children, saying he would never be permitted to meet her own and urging him to seek professional help. Related Article Royal family Meghan’s estranged father investigated over alleged child abuse images: report A friend of the Duchess of Sussex said: “She’s obviously upset and really frustrated that, having effectively been told to stay quiet and having been given assurances it would be investigated, it appears nothing was done. “She’s obviously pleased that the Met is now considering referring itself to the police watchdog.” The police force now faces questions about why information contained in a letter, which a whistleblower close to the Markle family sent to the Met’s Fixated Threat Assessment Centre, was not shared, and whether opportunities were missed to prevent further harm to children.



After receiving the letter, Scotland Yard passed it to royal protection officers, who shared it with the duchess. When she asked at the time what she should do about it, she was assured that “it was all in hand” and that to act could prejudice further investigations, the Telegraph says. When news of the letter’s existence emerged on Friday (UK time), the Met contacted the duchess’s office to ask whether she had retained a copy because they could not find the original. The Sussexes supplied them with it. One source told the Telegraph: “Thankfully, the duke and duchess are good record keepers and still had it.” Dai Davies, the former head of Scotland Yard’s Royal Protection Command, said he was “gobsmacked” that the Met had not contacted any other law enforcement bodies about the allegations.



Speaking to the Telegraph he said: “I’m frankly astounded that, having received this material, they did not contact other relevant forces. One of their roles is to protect the reputation of the royal family against any allegations. Meghan’s relationship with her father, a former Hollywood lighting director, became estranged around the time of her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018. AP “I believe they had a duty of care not only to Meghan but to any alleged victims to investigate. They would have been duty-bound, especially given Harry and Meghan’s level of fame just after their marriage, to carry out their own initial assessment and, if necessary, take it forward.” Davies added: “The allegations that her father was alleged to be a paedophile would have made them duty-bound to liaise with Harry’s protection team, the FBI and other police forces, where the alleged offences were said to have taken place. “It frankly beggars belief that they didn’t contact any other law enforcement agencies. I’m gobsmacked that they didn’t.”



Davies also expressed surprise that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex did not appear to have followed up the allegations against Thomas Markle Snr that they had received from the Met. Related Article Royal family Meghan reveals allegations against her father were reported to police in 2018 “This would have been the obvious thing to do, especially as they shortly after went on to have children of their own,” he said. A former senior Met detective told the Telegraph: “There is a very simple mechanism for passing this kind of information on to Interpol. You would grade the intelligence received and pass it through the National Crime Agency to Interpol. “It’s a bit surprising someone hasn’t said, ‘we need to pass this on to Interpol’, given the seriousness of the allegations concerning a relative of a member of the royal family.”



It emerged on Thursday that police in the Philippines were investigating Markle Snr, 82, for allegedly possessing “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images that had been found in recent months. The Sun reported that one of the images under investigation allegedly showed the duchess’s father having sex with a girl who appeared to be underage. In a statement on Friday, the duchess said she had received a letter in the summer of 2018 making “troubling and disturbing allegations” about her father. Scotland Yard said it had received the letter in January 2019. A spokesman for the duchess said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.” The Telegraph has since seen the letter to confirm its existence and the details of the “disturbing” claims within it.



‘I could never do what I’m accused of’ Thomas Markle Snr has denied the allegations, saying: “I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.” Related Video Video icon 4:00 Family friend reported Meghan’s father to police near royal wedding On Saturday, a police spokesman said: “Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the UK. “It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.



“The letter was reviewed, and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.” The FBI has said it is “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities”. “We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law,” a spokesman added. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Dalifornia: China’s mountain escape route for burnt-out youth
World.content:
Mona, a vocal artist, is setting up a nomadic-style community in Dali, where she hosts singing retreats.

With China’s economy slowing and youth unemployment rising, exhausted, disillusioned young people are seeking relief from the grinding pressures of modern life.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Dali, Yunnan: In the misty foothills of Dali’s Cangshan Mountain range, Mona is building a sanctuary of sorts for China’s burnt-out generations. On a parcel of unploughed farmland, where she lives for half the year in a Mongolian yurt with unpredictable electricity and free-range geese, she hosts singing retreats, guiding disquieted souls in sound healing and meditation to the beat of her shamanic drum. She’s building more yurts to establish a nomadic-style community, where people can stay for a few weeks or more to recharge their batteries. Her retreats draw an eclectic mix, including a few foreigners, but mostly they are city-weary Chinese, seeking relief from the grinding pressures of modern life. “If you don’t have your goals here, you will easily lose yourself,” Mona says. Fairfax Media “I’ve been seeing so many people who are working in cities, or their lives are so hard and so crazy,” says Mona, 34, who splits her time between Dali and Shanghai. Like many people in Dali, she prefers being known only by her first name. “They press [down] their emotions and their thinking. They never talk to their family or their colleagues. Eventually, they get bad depression.” Here in Dali, she says, people want to find another way to live.



It’s what has made Dali a sought-after refuge in China, where room for offbeat creativity and expression has narrowed over the past decade as authorities tightened their vision of an ideal society – one grounded in conformity, national security, traditional gender roles and hard work. Sometimes nicknamed Dalifornia, this mountain town in the country’s south-western Yunnan province has long been an escape route for China’s drifters and dreamers, its musicians and creatives. For decades, they have gravitated here to live in alternative communities of like-minded folk on the fringes of Dali’s touristy old town district. The rent is cheap, and the town’s traditional courtyard-style homes built by the local ethnic Bai people are conducive to communal living. However, since about 2021, when China’s economic miracle began faltering, a new influx of exhausted, disillusioned youth began arriving. And they’ve never stopped coming. They are the Millennials and Gen Z adults for whom the trusted recipe for upward mobility – the one their parents used to stride into China’s burgeoning middle classes in the 1990s and 2000s: studying hard and working hard – has crashed up against a domestic economic downturn and changing expectations of what constitutes a meaningful life. Youth unemployment is closing in on 20 per cent, as China’s labour market struggles to absorb 12 million new graduates from its universities each year, fuelling intense competition for limited white-collar jobs.



It’s now common to find graduates working as delivery drivers for takeaway food platforms alongside millions of farmers-turned-migrant workers who have left rural areas searching for better pay. However, the influx has fuelled intense competition in these jobs too, adding to the downward pressure on wages. The swelling gig economy has also propped up a broader unemployment rate of around 5 per cent, which some economists suspect is probably double that, and masks a level of precarity among the masses. In January, Goldman Sachs assessed that corporate hiring in China had fallen to its most depressed level in more than a decade, outside the COVID-19 period. While tech and AI industries are booming, they are not yet major job creators, and are unable to plug the economic rout caused by China’s property market collapse, which wiped out large swaths of middle-class wealth, paralysing consumer spending and investment. Life coach Coco, 32, first arrived in Dali five years ago, after quitting her job at Chinese tech company Alibaba due to exhaustion. Fairfax Media “Many people who come to Dali now, it’s because the economy is doing poorly, and they may have already been laid off by their companies,” says Coco, a former sales representative at Chinese tech giant Alibaba. “They figure there’s nothing else they can do anyway, so they just come to Dali to first find themselves, or simply to take a break for a while.” Others have trickled into Dali to escape the strictures of tradition and societal expectations that demanded certain things of them by 30 years old – a stable career, marriage, kids. For Chinese women, the verdict is harsher.



Enter your 30s single and unmarried, and you’re “sheng nu” – a leftover woman. Coco first arrived in Dali five years ago, among the early waves of corporate refugees who came to the mountains to escape the infamous 996 work culture (9am to 9pm, six days a week) rife in China’s tech industries. The practice still lingers, despite being ruled illegal by the courts, as the unspoken playbook to prove your value in ultra-competitive workplaces. She has reinvented herself as a life coach, channelling her experience with corporate exhaustion into seminars and one-on-one video sessions streamed from her rented courtyard house – an example of the new unconventional jobs that have currency in Dali’s alternative economy. In Dali, digital nomads and creatives live alongside people from the traditional ethnic Bai minority group. Fairfax Media “It’s very hard for our young generation because you just follow society’s clock,” Coco says. “In our traditional education system, we do not have too much time or energy to think about what’s [the value of] your life. We just focus on the exam scores, your university major and the job.” Burnt-out and burning through savings



The Connected Youth Community on the outskirts of Dali’s old town district is a flame that draws all moths, and the stepping-off point for many before they settle in for the longer term. It has all the hallmarks of a good hostel – cheap rooms, a fire pit, a shared pantry and a 24-hour bar out the front. In the communal area, the walls are plastered with posters advertising group philosophy sessions and talk therapy classes where people are encouraged to explore their authentic selves. The shared bookshelves are stocked with enlightenment thinkers and feminist texts, with Simone de Beauvoir’s The Second Sex and Virginia Woolf’s To the Lighthouse displayed as recommended reading. Outside a lot of dorm rooms, someone has abandoned a copy of Friedrich Nietzsche’s The Will to Power, an opus that may find new audiences among the modern mantras of self-actualisation and controlling your destiny. Young people take part in an AI workshop at the Connected Youth Community hostel in Dali. Fairfax Media Dali has a “free, tolerant, and open atmosphere, which is very rare in China”, says Paul, a Dali long-termer, who sometimes drops into the hostel to meet friends or attend group sessions. “Here, we are not bound by many restrictive ideas, and people won’t be quick to judge others.” At 36, Paul has earned a string of qualifications – including an expensive master’s degree in design from Monash University – only to be treading water in Dali with no stable employment. He was churned out of high-pressure jobs in Beijing and Shanghai, and is now exploring how to get by as a freelance tutor, hoping never again to set foot in a traditional workplace.

World.title: Selectors’ disdain for Sheffield Shield is sabotaging the Test team
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket Opinion Selectors’ disdain for Sheffield Shield is sabotaging the Test team Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist October 25, 2026 — 9:30am

October 25, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In an attempt to put the crushing second Test loss to South Africa into perspective, Pat Cummins said the result might be a good thing if it could “kick the side into gear”, and that perhaps the victory in Durban the previous week had papered over some hefty cracks. Was the captain trying to do an England on us and claim a moral victory when the scorecard told a very different story? Pat Cummins in the second Test. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe I can’t remember a loss by an innings in what was effectively a three-and-half-day match – after winning the toss, sending the opponent in and getting the best of both the bowling and batting conditions – having been presented as having an upside. Cummins was correct about the wallpaper, though.



“Bowlers win games, batters save them” has been a cricket adage since WG Grace replaced the bails, and this Australian squad has worn that maxim out. And why not, when you have four or five of the world’s best doing their thing? Temba Bavuma batting with the lower order saved South Africa from a sub-200 innings, and then his bowlers did the winning. Loading Australia’s decision to pick a bespoke attack sans Nathan Lyon and his 573 Test wickets proved to be an error of judgment. As Bavuma dug in with his lower order, Cummins searched for variety and had to settle for the truly part-time spin of Matt Renshaw, Nic Maddinson and Marnus Labuschagne. It did not work. Beau Webster kept the runs down, but didn’t look like making a breakthrough.



Cummins did catch Lyon’s eye, but only because he was wearing hi-vis and delivering comestibles at the boundary’s edge. All he lacked was a scooter, funky helmet and a loose regard for the road rules to complete his newest role. Australia’s batsmen had excellent conditions in which to grind past the follow-on, reassess the time and how the pitch might be changing under the South African sun. But they could not save the game. Anrich Nortje (right) celebrates taking the wicket of Marnus Labuschagne in Australia’s first dig in Gqeberha. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Travis Head played an excellent innings within the confines of his most ebullient strokeplay but eventually fell again to the ball moving into him, dragging on for the umpteenth time – on this occasion with the wicketkeeper standing up and restricting his mental space as much as the physical. Australia are the No.1 ranked Test team because of their bowling and in spite of their batting.



The batting order and personnel have been much debated, but you can’t put players in a structure if you aren’t sure of their actual skills, and their skills are measurably different depending on cricket education and experience. They can’t all bat at five, so it is a blessing Steve Smith is now (after the twilight zone opening experiment) first inked on the team sheet at No.4. Sure, he batted at seven in the second innings, but that was due to the employment of a nightwatchman and a neck twinge, and it failed miserably. So back to second drop in Cape Town. Maddinson’s selection has rendered the entire Sheffield Shield competition irrelevant. Why does the best batsman in the world come in at seven when the captain reckons he was fit to bat the night before? Perhaps it was not the best use of resources. Selecting four No.5s sounds great, but someone has to open and someone with some basic batting form and technique has to bat No.3. Which brings back the circular and by now hackneyed argument over Labuschagne’s tenure, and puts the spotlight on Maddinson’s elevation from domestic 50-over cricket to opening in a Test match against a top-line attack.



Labuschagne is no longer a lame duck, he’s a dead one. His time is up. He is not producing and hasn’t done so for a number of years. Cummins says Labuschagne is “hitting the ball well”. That notion is open to dispute, but even if we concede for the sake of argument that Cummins is on the money, the bottom line for any batsmen in any era is “how many” rather than “how”. Skill is a precursor to performance. Marnus is not performing. This is selection 101, whereas you would have to write a new “concept” chapter to find any text for Maddinson’s return to Test cricket. His selection has rendered the entire Sheffield Shield competition irrelevant. Maddinson did not play any Shield last season and had minimal underperforming appearances the year before. Recovery from serious health concerns naturally took precedence, although he was slated for a return as NSW captain this summer before being called to Africa.



The message sent to every budding Test player, which should be just about everyone plying their trade in the cricket world’s premier first-class competition, is that the national selectors don’t care what you are doing, how intensely you are competing, or how you deliver in the varying environments served up around the country. George Bailey, Tony Dodemaide, Andrew McDonald and Cummins (on tour) have such a low regard for the competition which has been the staple for Test selection for 130 years that they will pick from whatever white-ball competition happens to be flogging bowlers. Nic Maddinson scored four runs across two innings in the second Test against South Africa in Gqeberha. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Even more bizarre was the suggestion from Cummins that Mitchell Marsh was in line for the first Test even though he had retired from first-class cricket. At least Maddinson was still on a playing roster. When Dodemaide was the general manger of Cricket Victoria, he championed a move for the Sheffield Shield to be restricted to one round because the costs were too great to justify a home and way profile.



Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Australia’s patched-up batting has reached boiling point. It must change for Cape Town In focussing on the cost, he was ignoring the value of the competition. The Maddinson selection (and the Marsh intonation) is a bold, underlined, italicised manifestation of that thought process. Under Dodemaide’s proposal, the burden of forming a Test team would then fall on performances in T20, 50-over and club cricket. A non-competitive Test team would lose support, attendances and sponsorships, media rights would fade away and the Shield would lose funding. A self-fulfilling prophecy. On the brighter side, the Shield is going gangbusters in the first couple of rounds, with young guns and veterans making runs and taking wickets and some thrilling results to boot. Might be an idea if the national selectors took note, or CA employed some people who will. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Italian police wield batons, French fire tear gas at latest protests
World.content:
WorldEuropeParis protests Italian police wield batons, French fire tear gas at latest protests David Crowe October 25, 2026 — 7:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: Police have clashed with protesters in France and Italy during massive rallies one week after similar gatherings descended into riots and looting in major cities. Officers wielded batons against some of the protesters in Turin to prevent crowds from coming close to stores, highlighting anxiety about a repeat of the destruction witnessed on city streets one week earlier. Loading Protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum in Rome, but police escorted them out, while others held a peaceful protest in the Italian capital. The protests in France, meanwhile, were smaller and less violent than those seen on the previous weekend, when authorities estimated that 3000 stores were damaged or looted.



A man lies on the ground as police in Turin take on demonstrators during protest against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services during one of several protests across Italy. Mauro Ujetto/LaPresse via AP The French government estimated that about 410,000 people joined the protests in various cities on Saturday, down from an estimated 550,000 who took to the streets across the country the previous Saturday. A group of protesters shield themselves from a water cannon during a protest on the streets of Paris. Getty Images In Paris, students and union members joined a demonstration along a route agreed with authorities from Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes, east of the city centre and distant from areas looted the previous weekend. Most of the protest was peaceful, but some vandals tried to break into a car dealership, the Parisian police said in a statement.



“The numerous checks carried out in transportation systems deterred potential looters from converging on Paris,” the police said. Protesters dressed as Spider-Man attend a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France. AP Photo/Jeremias Gonzalez About 110,000 people joined the Paris march, according to the police, who released photographs of home-made weapons such as blocks of timber with nails attached, which they confiscated from some of those in the crowd. Left-wing presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon marched in the Paris demonstration, while right-wing presidential candidate Marine Le Pen went ahead with the annual congress of her party, National Rally, despite protests outside the venue in the city of Orleans. While authorities sought to ban rallies in cities including Marseilles and Lyon, some protesters gathered there and elsewhere to declare support for freedom of speech and freedom to demonstrate. Police used tear gas against protesters in Paris, Lyon and other cities.



Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at least 1000 people were arrested at the events across the country on Saturday, speaking at about 8pm on Saturday night (5am on Sunday, AEST). He said the number was likely to increase. There were more than 2700 arrests during the riots and looting on the previous weekend. Nunez accused far-left activists and criminal gangs of causing trouble. “In almost ​every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of ⁠violence,” he said. View post on X



Separately, investigators revealed more details of the gunman alleged to have killed one victim and wounded five others in suburbs to the south-west of Paris, naming him as Kevin T without disclosing his surname. They said the suspect, 39, had a criminal history and lived in the area near the shootings. The investigators said the alleged killer had sought to target others by fitting his apartment with three gas cylinders and electrical wires connected to a timer. While attention has focused on France over the past week because of the scale of the looting and violence, similar protests in Italy led to looting in Milan and clashes with police in several cities. Police named a freelance journalist, Youssef Siher, as a key organiser of a new October 17 movement that aimed to continue the protests and confront authorities, according to reports in national newspaper La Repubblica and other media outlets. Siher was described as a 30-year-old second-generation Italian from Brescia, a pro-Palestine activist and co-ordinator of the protests.



While progressive activists dominated many protests, a right-wing rally assembled in Rome with a call to “unblock everything” and oppose those who were bringing city streets to a standstill or looting shops. Related Article Protests Just what do France’s angry youth want? It’s complicated “We reject the permanent, fruitless and ideological confrontation of the youth left,” said the rally organised by student members of Azione, a centrist party whose name translates as “Action”. Protesters gathered in cities ranging from Brussels to Madrid and Lisbon to demand government action on the cost of living, with housing costs a particular concern in Spain and Portugal. While police in Lisbon and Porto cleared protest encampments in recent days, many protesters returned to continue campaigning for policies to ease the cost of housing.



In Madrid, the scene of massive rallies over housing in recent weeks, people gathered on Saturday to call for more protection for pensions. Spanish unions are planning a general strike on November 11 to galvanise protest over living conditions ahead of the country’s parliamentary elections on November 29, to decide whether Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez remains in power. Related Article Analysis

Paris protests The violence of the streets of Paris looked like rage. It revealed a society that will take years to heal While several European countries experienced protests on Saturday, they differed in scale and underlying issues. In Albania, protesters gathered in the capital, Tirana, to oppose Prime Minister Edi Rama, who is facing accusations of corruption. In Serbia, tens of thousands of people attended student rallies on Thursday to urge a vote against the country’s strongman leader, Aleksandar Vucic, at elections on Sunday.

World.title: Sydney to host Super Netball grand final for first time
World.content:
SportNetballSuper Netball Sydney to host Super Netball grand final for first time Frances Howe October 25, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The last time Sydney netball fans had the chance to support a home team in a league grand final was 18 years ago in the former ANZ Championship. The Super Netball league was nearly a decade away from foundation when a six-year-old Amy Sligar, who now plays for the Sydney Sirens, watched the NSW Swifts defeat the Waikato Bay of Plenty Magic 65-56 in July 2008. Sydney will host the Super League netball grand final next year, much to the delight of Amy Sligar from the Sydney Sirens, Grace Whyte from the Swifts and Netball Australia boss Mark Falvo. James Brickwood “I would have watched that game with stars in my eyes and probably my heroes were playing in that game,” she said. Though the Swifts would appear in two more grand finals of the ANZ Championship and go on to play in three of the Super Netball grand finals since the league began in 2017 none were in Sydney. Neither were the two other grand finals a Sydney team featured in.



But Sligar, now 24, has the chance to play a final at home in 2027. On Sunday, Netball Australia and the NSW government will announce that the 2027 grand final will be held on July 31 at Afterpay Arena at Sydney Olympic Park, the same venue will then host the Netball World Cup a month later. The Adelaide Thunderbirds celebrate their 2026 Super Netball title win in Melbourne. Getty Images “Netball is one of the biggest participation sports in NSW, with thousands of kids and adults taking to the court every week, and it deserves the same attention and support we give our other major sport,” NSW Premier Chris Minns said on Sunday. “For too long, we haven’t invested enough in netball and we’re working to change that – from grassroots facilities and participation right through to bringing the biggest events in the sport to NSW.”



The state government expects the grand final will bring 8000 spectators to Sydney to watch at the 18,000-capacity arena, adding what they estimate to be more than $4 million to the economy. The World Cup in August will see a target of 200,000 attendees to watch Australia’s Diamonds defend their 2023 title. The state government has also set up a $1.5 million World Cup legacy program for players, coaches and officials. Minister for Sport Steve Kamper said the events would make the city the centre of the netball world next year. Netball Australia chief executive Mark Falvo said 2027 will be huge for netball fans in Sydney. Sligar said knowing the grand final will be held at home provides extra motivation for the season ahead, especially over local rivals the Swifts.



“My first reaction is that it makes me want to make the grand final even more to have a home grand final,” she said. “You almost couldn’t write a better script to have a new Sydney team [the Sirens] and then Sydney hosting the grand final, Sydney hosting the World Cup this year.” “I think for young boys and girls and men and women to be able to come and see the world’s best netball, it just builds excitement on the sport.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘National suicide’: The election issue tearing Israelis apart
World.content:
A row over whether a Jerusalem coffee shop could open on the Sabbath escalated into an epic culture war. For modern Israel, it could be the shape of things to come.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Jerusalem/ Bnei Brak: Almost anywhere else in the world, a cafe opening for business on Saturday would not be an inflammatory act. But in downtown Jerusalem, Cafe Basimta’s decision to sell coffee and pastries on the Sabbath ignited an almighty culture war between the Holy City’s ultra-Orthodox and secular residents. Soon after the coffee shop opened in a quiet alley in May, dozens of ultra-Orthodox teenage boys wearing black suits and fedoras showed up to block its entrance while chanting “Whoever breaks the Sabbath has no part in the world to come”. A young ultra-Orthodox protester stands his ground outside Cafe Basimta while counter-protesters make their point. The cafe has now decided to stay shut on Saturdays. AFP Ultra-Orthodox Jews believe in resting on the Sabbath, the frequent study of religious texts, strict gender segregation and eating kosher, pitting them against the less devout, who favour a more relaxed approach. As the demonstrations grew each week, so did counter-protests. Hundreds of non-religious activists locked arms to protect the entrance to the café, and prominent politicians from the right and left joined in. The fact that the cafe’s owners – the messianic and controversial Jews for Jesus organisation – were hardly secular was a wrinkle in the narrative. But it didn’t deter most of the counter-protesters, who believed they were fighting for an important principle. The argument raging over whether coffee and pastries could be sold on the Jewish sabbath became a microcosm of a wider debate about competing rights in modern Israel. AFP



“We see it as our right to be able to drink coffee on the Sabbath in the centre of Jerusalem,” says deputy Jerusalem mayor Adir Schwarz, a champion of the city’s secular population. “Our capital is supposed to unite all Israelis, and if any Jew is being pushed out of Jerusalem, that is a bad forewarning for the rest of the state of Israel.” While the havoc was a boon for business, the owners ultimately decided it wasn’t worth the pain. In September, the cafe announced it would no longer open on Saturdays. “The cafe has become, over the past several months, a focal point of friction and danger,” Jews for Jesus chief executive Eli Birnbaum said. Strict ultra-Orthodox modesty laws have brought the community into conflict with the 21st century. Disappointed by the decision, secular activists mostly abandoned the cafe and business plummeted. When we visited last week, the coffee was excellent, but only a handful of customers were there. Schwarz says the backdown was just the latest blow to secular Jerusalemites, who feel increasingly marginalised and disempowered. Ultra-Orthodox residents are rising in number and moving into secular suburbs, sparking heated battles over resources and cultural norms. ‘We live in separate worlds, and those worlds are getting further apart’ Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser “A territorial battle is playing out in certain neighbourhoods as their identity changes and becomes more religious,” Schwarz says.



Schwarz cites strict ultra-Orthodox modesty laws which can expose female pedestrians to harassment and intimidation for wearing jeans. “The fact a secular woman cannot walk in pants through the neighbourhood she grew up in is a big problem,” Schwarz argues. Children in Bnei Brak. The birthrate for ultra-Orthodox Jews now vastly exceeds that of other groups. Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community – known as the Haredim – makes up 14 per cent of the national population. That figure is exploding, reflecting the fact that the birth rate for ultra-Orthodox women (6.5 children per woman) is vastly higher than for other Jewish women (2.2 children). By 2065, the Haredim are projected to comprise a third of Israeli society, a figure unimaginable when Israel was founded in 1948. Such rapid growth equals more political power but also greater scrutiny about ultra-Orthodox Jews’ contribution to Israeli society. Twenty minutes from central Tel Aviv, Bnei Brak is a world away from modern Israel. The fight over Cafe Basimta is emblematic of a deeper battle being waged in Israel ahead of national elections on Tuesday. Topics that foreigners may expect to be front-of-centre – like how Israel waged its war on Gaza or the possibility of a two-state solution with the Palestinians – are almost entirely absent from the public discourse. Meanwhile, the concessions provided to ultra-Orthodox Israelis are tearing the nation apart and dominating the campaign. Bnei Brak is a mere 20-minute drive from the gay bars and non-kosher restaurants of Tel Aviv, but it might as well be on a different planet. “We live in separate worlds, and those worlds are getting further apart,” Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser says of the two cities, which serve as avatars for Israel’s ultra-Orthodox and secular tribes. Here there is none of the clashing and intermingling you find in more integrated Jerusalem. Bnei Brak Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser says he is alarmed by the push for compulsory military service for the ultra-Orthodox community, who are currently exempt. Vered Adir



Bnei Brak is one of the world’s most densely populated cities: 230,000 people, almost all of them Haredi, crammed into just seven square kilometres of land. “It’s a terrible city, it’s dirty, it’s more crowded than Gaza,” Goldwasser says as he slurps a bowl of matzo ball soup. His kosher phone, which blocks internet access, sits on the table. On the plus side, he says it is a self-contained society packed with restaurants, yeshivas, shops and medical facilities where the streets remain lively until the early hours of the morning. In Hebrew, the Haredim means those who tremble before God. To be ultra-Orthodox is to be on edge. But Goldwasser says the community’s naturally high anxiety has spiked to intolerable levels because of an all-out campaign to force them to serve in the military. The dilemma of ultra-Orthodox army service has existed before the founding of Israel in 1948. To ensure as broad support as possible for the creation of a Jewish state, founding prime minister David Ben-Gurion granted 400 yeshiva students exemptions from compulsory military service. This reflected the ultra-Orthodox community’s fraught relationship with Zionism (many believe establishing a sovereign Jewish state before the arrival of the Messiah violates divine law). Related Article Exclusive

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Like a wounded animal’: Netanyahu will do whatever it takes to stay in power, former PM warns A decade later, with thousands of students now exempt, Ben-Gurion questioned his decision. Today, court filings by Israel’s attorney-general estimate that about 80,000 are avoiding military service. This became a source of fury as Israel fought a multi-front war against its enemies after the October 7 attacks of 2023. The burdens of service – time spent away from family and the risk of dying on the battlefield – have not been distributed evenly across society. Reflecting the new era Israel entered after October 7, the Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that the longstanding blanket exemption for yeshiva students was unlawful. Fierce resistance has followed. Last year, chief rabbi Yitzhak Yosef used his weekly sermon to warn that the ultra-Orthodox community “will all board planes and leave Israel” if they are forced to serve in the army.



Attempts to force Haredi men to enlist, including through arrests, have sparked riots and blockades of major highways. In June, ultra-Orthodox rioters smashed windows, damaged flowerpots, and vandalised a car parked at the home of the Supreme Court’s deputy president. Elchanan Wasserman says his story proves you can be ultra-Orthodox and serve in the Israeli military. “As far as they’re concerned, it’s life or death. Religion comes first,” Wasserman says, explaining why the issue arouses such passion. Bnei Brak yeshiva student Yakov, 20, says he has no intention of enlisting. “Prison, sanctions, nothing can break us,” he declares. His dream is to be a rabbi. Protests and arrests have accelerated in the lead-up to the October 27 election, raising the temperature. The military arrested 40 ultra-Orthodox men returning from the United States on Tuesday at Tel Aviv airport on suspicion of draft dodging. An ultra-Orthodox Jew burns an Israeli flag as anti-government amid protests against their military service exemptions. Getty Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose conservative coalition is reliant on ultra-Orthodox parties, criticised the arrests. “We need to preserve the world of Torah study because it has preserved us,” he said in a radio interview. On the other side of the debate, the four main Jewish parties running against Netanyahu are all campaigning to end sweeping exemptions from military service. They are convinced they are onto a vote winner. An overwhelming 72 per cent of Israelis want to see the Haredim drafted alongside other Israelis eligible for military service, according to a September poll by the Israel Democracy Institute.

World.title: ‘Without you the union is gone’: Mick Gatto’s secret support for John Setka
World.content:
Leaked texts reveal how John Setka raged, survived and stayed at the top of the CFMEU through a domestic violence scandal, with unwavering support from his gangland friend and some Labor insiders.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The sky was a blanket of unrelenting grey and large droplets clung to the leaves of the red flowering gums lining the road in Melbourne’s west as a thickset man with thinning hair scrolled through his mobile phone. Australia’s most powerful union leader wanted advice. If anyone knew how to navigate bad press and criminal allegations it was Domenic “Mick” Gatto. Any other union or political leader facing criminal accusations of stalking and terrorising their wife would have been penning their resignation letter. But not the towering trade union chief now focused on his phone. As usual, the boss of Australia’s construction union, a division of the CFMEU, was defiant. And why wouldn’t he be? He was John Setka, son of a blue-collar worker who in 1970, when John was only six, had survived one of Australia’s worst industrial accidents. John’s dad had ridden a slab of the West Gate Bridge as it plummeted through nearly 50 metres of icy Melbourne air. The same slab of concrete and iron had claimed the lives of 35 others. Forty years after his father’s escape from death, John Setka had led tens of thousands of chanting protesters through Melbourne’s CBD, unfazed by the cops on horseback or those sweating on foot in their riot gear. Setka at the 2018 ALP conference in Adelaide, two days before he stormed out. Alex Ellinghausen In 2018, he had stormed out of the national conference of Australia’s oldest political party having labelled its former leader Kevin Rudd a “f---ing dog” and a “maggot” as the ex-prime minister was awarded his Labor Party life membership. The rain was still falling, the sky growing ever greyer. Setka knew his so-called union comrades were now judging him. F--- ’em. Setka tapped furiously on his phone. “F--- these prim and proper people have never done it hard in the [sic] whole lives,” Setka texted his mate. “I’m sick of all these squareheads trying to micro manage me and tell me who I can be seen with or who I can talk to. Yet when the shit hits the fan they’re nowhere to be seen.”





And yet, behind the scenes, it wasn’t all bad for Setka. He was also fielding support, and not only from Mick Gatto. It said something of Setka’s power and reach that it wasn’t just several of his male comrades offering him backroom support, but women too. Even when Albanese was the newly installed opposition leader and moved to turf Setka from the party, Setka’s phone had lit up with text messages from female federal and state Labor politicians and union figures. Victorian MP Bronwyn Halfpenny had assured Setka she was “thinking of you and hope everything will be OK”. She had texted: “You are a great comrade to working people so the establishment will always want to bring u down. Hope to see you soon. Xxx.” Rail, Tram and Bus Union secretary Luba Grigorovitch (now a state Labor MP and minister) had repeatedly sent messages of support, vowing to direct her union to back Setka. “We will get through this John xx,” she had promised. From left: former CFMEU official Derek Christopher, state Labor MP Luba Grigorovitch, an unidentified supporter and Setka at a 2024 CFMEU event. Instagram Grigorovitch advised Setka to rely on the behind-the-scenes advice of communications expert and Labor political adviser Tanja Kovac, who also headed EMILY’s List, a group devoted to promoting ALP women into parliament. Kovac had also texted Setka, telling him to craft his public messaging carefully. Setka had decided to plead guilty to a charge of harassment and breaching a family violence order, but Kovac warned Setka that he not only had to survive the Magistrates’ Court but the court of public opinion as well. It was vital that Setka be seen to publicly champion “the need to talk about family and gendered violence”, texted Kovac. “Be strong, genuine, sorry & the leader I know you are,” she had advised, finishing her text with the words: “Thinking of you.” Kovac also suggested that Setka find supporters willing to support him publicly. Mick Gatto required no cajoling. Of all Setka’s backers, he had been the most unflinching. Gatto was, in underworld parlance, staunch. Where Kovac urged Setka to display contrition, Gatto urged him to fight. “Sorry you are going through all this nonsense. If I was you I would reconsider pleading guilty,” Gatto advised.



Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad ‘Trading drugs for weapons’: Police charge CFMEU delegate over union HQ deals Governments and the “establishment” had also come after him, Gatto told Setka. They had changed the law to stop him from running his boxing promotion company. Now they were coming after Setka because of all he had done for the hundreds of thousands of building workers around the country. Gatto wasn’t having any of it. “Thanks john for publicly defending our friendship,” he texted. “I do love ya. Without you the union is gone.” Setka hadn’t bothered to respond to some of his other supporters, but for Gatto he had only love. “Thanks brother. I really appreciate the support and I’ll never forget it,” he told his ally. Setka’s union would also not forget Gatto’s support. A month after Setka took to the steps of the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court, with Emma by his side, to publicly “take responsibility” for the criminal harassment and intimidation of his wife, another man appeared on the steps of the neighbouring Supreme Court. Gangland identity Faruk Orman had just been released from prison, his murder conviction quashed after a court had found he’d been denied a fair trial because his lawyer engaged in serious misconduct. Nick McKenzie and Ben Schneiders’ book. Before being jailed for 12 years, Orman had worked as Mick Gatto’s driver. But it was the accusation that he had acted as the wheelman for an underworld hitman that had landed Orman in prison. Orman had entered prison with a boyish face and a skinny frame; he’d left with jowls, a slight paunch, and no desire to drive any more gangland figures around town.

World.title: Woman whose cancer was almost missed wants breast density reporting in screening
World.content:
A woman whose breast cancer was not detected after a mammogram, is calling for more information around dense breast tissue.

Dionne Scott, from Whanganui, was diagnosed in 2024 at the age of 50.

She had found a lump in her breast that was not detected during a routine mammogram nine months earlier.

Six months later, with the lump still there, she returned to her GP and was referred for another mammogram and an ultrasound.

Neither identified the cancer, but because the lump could still be felt, Scott insisted on having a biopsy.

The biopsy revealed breast cancer, and Scott underwent a lumpectomy, followed by radiation and hormone treatment.

"If I hadn't pushed and said, yeah, I want the biopsy, if I just said, okay, I'll wait another year, I'm sure it would have been way more than grade two," she said.

It is estimated that one in 10 women have extremely dense breasts, like Scott.

For these women, standard mammograms may detect only around half of cancers.

The Breast Cancer Foundation said the current one-size-fits-all approach had failed them.

Chief executive Vanessa Sorenson said that while mammograms were the best screening tool for most women, they were not effective for everyone, and there was no publicly funded additional screening for women with dense breasts based on their risk.

Breast Cancer Foundation chief executive Vanessa Sorenson Supplied / Breast Cancer Foundation

"Breast density puts women at higher risk of developing breast cancer, while also making cancer harder to see on a mammogram," she said.

"Yet women are not routinely told about their density through the public screening programme."

Scott said if she had known that having dense breasts both increased her risk of breast cancer and made cancers harder to see on a mammogram, she would have paid for additional testing privately.

Sorenson said she was not alone.

"We're increasingly hearing from women whose cancers were not detected on mammograms and who only learnt after diagnosis that they have dense breasts.

"Women have a right to know about their breast density, but information must be matched with access to screening that is appropriate for their risk."

As part of the Breast Cancer Foundation's 2026 Election Manifesto, it is calling on the next government to:

require BreastScreen Aotearoa to include breast density in every screening result;

fund additional screening for women identified as having a higher risk of breast cancer; and

begin a phased rollout of contrast-enhanced mammography, where clinically appropriate.

Sorenson said contrast-enhanced mammography, or CEM, used a contrast dye to help make cancers more visible.

Research showed it could detect cancers in dense breast tissue that may be difficult to see on a standard mammogram.

AFP

"We've all got very different breasts. And for women that have very, very high density, when you have a mammogram, which is still incredibly important, your tumours with dense breast tissue show up white. So they can't be seen," she said.

"We're really also looking to pull forward contrast-enhanced mammography, or CEM. It's a type of mammogram that uses injected contrast dye. And that way, it actually makes areas of unusual blood flow more visible, helping radiologists identify possible cancers."

Sorenson said women needed political parties to move beyond recognising the problem and commit to addressing it:

"Telling women their density is only the first step. Reporting should begin as soon as possible, alongside work to determine what screening women at higher risk should receive.

"Without a funded pathway, women who can afford to pay privately may be able to access additional screening, while others can't. A woman's ability to get the screening she needs should be based on her clinical risk, not her bank balance."

Breast density reporting is increasingly becoming standard practice internationally.

It is mandatory at the federal level in the United States and largely standardised or required across most provinces and territories in Canada, Sorenson said.

Australia has been introducing reporting progressively across states, with women identified as having high breast density advised to discuss their overall risk and possible screening options with their GP, she added.

World.title: Opportunity to set up Future Generations Commissioner for government's long-term impacts
World.content:
The Opportunity Party will set up a Future Generations Commissioner tasked with holding governments to account for the long-term impacts of their policies and stop "short term thinking", if elected.

The party would enact a Future Generations Act giving the commissioner powers to guide development of long-term national goals.

The Commissioner would be appointed for a five-year term, and the position would have no minister and no party to direct its findings. Funding would be scrutinised through the Officers of Parliament process, not a minister.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said New Zealand needed to stop making decisions based on the next election.

"Governments come and go, priorities change, and long-term plans get thrown out. We put off investments we know we need to make, only to discover that fixing the problem later costs us far more."

"We can see the consequences all around us. Young people struggling to afford a home, infrastructure that's been neglected for decades, and a health system lurching from one crisis to the next." she said.

The Commissioner would also be responsible for assembling the party's proposed citizens' assemblies and other kinds of public participation in developing New Zealand's long-term goals - designed in partnership with Māori and consistent with Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

Major government policy, Budgets, and investment proposals would be required to disclose long-term costs, benefits, risks and impacts on future generations, including the cost of "doing nothing".

Wong said politicians were "very good at telling us what something will cost today" but not good at "telling us what it will cost our children if we fail to act".

She said the Commissioner would not replace elected representatives, but help ensure the interests of future generations were considered in their decisions.

"Democracy shouldn't just mean having a vote every three years. People should have a real say in the future we're building together."

World.title: Explainer: How to enrol to vote and why today is your final chance
World.content:
Explainer - Today is the final day to enrol to vote in this year's election.

Changes this year mean that enrolment closes 13 days before election day on 7 November.

If you haven't enrolled yet, you've got until midnight today.

Being on the voter roll is important for several reasons - and while it's rarely enforced, it's actually legally required that you enrol to vote if you're eligible.

Democracy - it's important and it's the law!

Why is today the deadline? Can't we enrol on election day?

As of this election, you can no longer enrol to vote all the way up to election day.

You must be registered no later than midnight, Sunday 25 October.

How to enrol to vote:

Visit the Electoral Commission website and put in your details.

There are fears that the changes could reduce voter turnout, especially among younger voters.

As of Friday, 92.4 percent of those eligible were enrolled, but only 69.9 percent of those aged 18-24 were enrolled.

The Electoral Commission is also running in-person voter enrolment events through today.

"This weekend, we'll be at events around the country to help people enrol or check their details. You can also drop off an enrolment form at one of our hubs," Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne told RNZ.

You can find a list of those enrolment hubs here.

Voting papers being printed in Petone, Wellington weeks ahead of the election. Samuel Rillstone/RNZ

What else is the electoral roll used for?

The electoral roll isn't just a list of who's enrolled to vote. It's also an important data resource.

"Beyond allowing people to vote at national and local elections, the electoral roll is very useful to Government for a range of reasons," University of Otago law professor Andrew Geddis said.

"It is used for jury selection, political campaigning purposes, and health and social science research."

The electoral roll contains your full name and home address and can be viewed at public libraries or Electoral Commission offices, and is also available for purchase.

"We do not release your date of birth, phone numbers or email address to the public," the commission says on its website.

But some of the information given to the roll can be released to other groups.

"The law requires us to give lists of people who are enrolled to vote on the published electoral rolls to certain people and organisations when they ask for them," Le Quesne said.

"These lists may have your personal information on them. This includes information that's not publicly available on the electoral rolls, such as date of birth or the age range you're in and whether you're of Māori descent."

However, there's also an unpublished roll you can request to be put on, which keeps all details private.

Information can be given to local councils for their elections, the Ministry of Justice for jury lists, Stats NZ and other organisations for research.

Political parties, candidates and MPs can also ask for lists of people who are enrolled for campaign uses - but the commission does not give out phone numbers or email addresses to them.

Voting papers being printed in Petone, Wellington weeks ahead of the election. Samuel Rillstone/RNZ

Did you know it's actually against the law not to be enrolled?

Under section 82 of the Electoral Act 1993, it's a legal requirement for anyone who is eligible to enrol once they turn 18.

The act states offenders might receive a fine of up to $100 or up to $200 for a second conviction if you don't have a good reason for not being enrolled.

But stand down - that basically never happens.

"There is a penalty but it's not just a matter of being unenrolled," said Le Quesne.

"It's an offence if a person knowingly or wilfully fails to apply to enrol - in other words really digs in their heels and refuses to enrol."

The Electoral Commission would much rather you just enrol, please.

"We're not aware of anyone being prosecuted for refusing to enrol," Le Quesne said.

"The Electoral Commission does not have the power to fine or prosecute anyone. We would need to refer a matter to police. It would be up to the police to decide whether any action is taken."

The courts also aren't likely to make a big deal of not being enrolled to vote.

"Enforcement of this measure requires a police prosecution in the District Court and I do not know of this ever occurring," said Geddis.

"I suspect the police have somewhat more urgent matters to attend to."

It's been compulsory to enrol in general electorates since 1924, and in the Maori electorates since 1956.

"The idea behind compulsory enrolment is that it is reasonable, in the interests of facilitating a healthy democracy, for the law to require those eligible to enrol," Geddis said.

"Making enrolment compulsory helps ensure the electoral roll is accurate and complete, which enables electoral officials to administer elections and to prevent and detect electoral manipulation."

Consider the law more of a friendly reminder, perhaps.

"The law effectively works more as a prompt to civic duty rather than a stick with which to beat people who fail to comply," Geddis said.

Does that mean it's mandatory to vote, too?

Actually, no.

"Enrolment is compulsory, but voting is not," Le Quesne said.

"Compulsory voting would then change voting from being a right, which people may or may not exercise, to a civic duty," Geddis said.

Across the ditch, it is mandatory to vote in Australia, where turnout typically runs about 90 percent for the last several federal elections. By comparison, 77.51 percent of those enrolled voted in our 2023 general election, according to the Electoral Commission.

An Independent Electoral Review conducted by the previous government was released in 2023, and recommended keeping compulsory enrolment on the books. It also looked at the lack of enforcement of that rule.

"There are good reasons for not strictly enforcing compulsory enrolment, including that strict enforcement may negatively impact people's experience of the electoral system," the report found.

That panel also looked at whether compulsory voting should be introduced as in Australia, but said it ultimately considered "that requiring people to vote may be a step too far, as it constrains freedom of choice."

World.title: National sets out first actions if re-elected in 100 day plan
World.content:
The National Party has released its 100 day plan, setting out the first actions it would take if re-elected.

The 26-point plan, compiling various announcements from the campaign, includes a commitment to introduce legislation to extend paid parental leave, update consent laws, and get the Commerce Commission to investigate the Foodstuffs split.

Other actions were already in-train, or required by a government, such as releasing a Budget Policy Statement.

It also contains a pledge to launch a trade mission to India, following the free trade agreement entering into force earlier this month.

Unveiling the plan at a rally in Browns Bay in Auckland, National leader Christopher Luxon said the election would be tight.

"Turning around Labour's mess was never going to be a three-year job and National needs more time to finish it. Our 100 Day Plan sets out what we will prioritise if re-elected to build on our progress."
